item.title: Octavus Insights Corner - Corporate Venture Capital (November 2026)
item.description: Octavus Insights Corner for November 2026: pharma corporate venture capital (Jan 2025 - Jul 2026), covering funding trends, the most active CVCs and the therapeutic areas attracting capital.
item.content:encoded:
Month: November 2026 Presenter: Team Octavus CORPORATE VENTURE Insights Corner CAPITAL (Jan 2025 - Jul 2026)

AGENDA Content INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Understanding the pharma CVC ecosystem Who is investing and where is the capital flowing? 05 07 Meet the leading pharma CVC players Where is pharma CVC capital being deployed? 12 16 Innovation hotspots and emerging technologies Strengths and risks of the CVC model What lies ahead for pharma CVCs? 19 23 25

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Highlights from AACR-25 (May, 25) US Tariff impact on Pharma industries (Jun, 25) EULAR-25: Key insights of Psoriatic Arthritis (Jul, 25) Antibody Drug Conjugate: The next big investment in Oncology (Aug, 25) Animal Health (Oct, 25) Obesity deep dive (Nov, 25) GLP-1 and GIP (Dec, 25) Hematological Highlights from ASH 2025 (Jan, 26) China Biotech’s Global Positioning from JPM-26 (Feb,26) BIOSIMILARS RISING: The Catalyst For A New Age In Biologics Therapies (Mar,26) Cell Therapy Within CGT (Apr, 26) Gene Therapy Within CGT (May, 26) Regulatory Designations US FDA & EMA (Jun, 26) RadioTherapy Highlights (Jul, 26) AI in Drug Development (Aug, 26) Companion Diagnostics (Sep, 26) RAS Inhibitors (Oct, 26) Additional: 1 Beautiful Bill PRIOR ISSUES INSIGHTS CORNER

Executive Summary Pharma is moving from VC to strategic capital: About 65% of 2023 new molecular entity (NME) launches were externally sourced, and partnered assets reach launch at 19% vs 9% for non-partnered ones INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com INSIGHTS CORNER Funding is active and getting larger: 161 disclosed deals raised ~$14.5B from Jan 2025 to Jul 2026. Follow-on rounds took 61% of the dollars and Q2 2026 was the peak at 35 deals and $3.5B CVC activity is concentrated, and CVCs mostly join rather than lead: Sanofi and Novo joined deals worth 45% of disclosed funding, and the top 5 CVCs are in 58% of rounds. Pharma CVCs led only about a quarter of rounds with a named lead, while VC/PE firms led 67% Four therapeutic areas take 78.5% of funding: Oncology leads with 28.3%, followed by Neurology 19.9%, Autoimmune/ Inflammation 16.3% and Cardio-metabolic 14.0%. Neurology surged to $1.0B in Q2 2026, and 25 mega-rounds of $150M+ or more hold 39% of the dollars Biologics and AI/ML are gaining: Monthly funding for AI/ML has doubled and for protein/ peptide/ other biologics has roughly tripled since H2 2025, while small molecules are down 55%. The outlook favors Oncology, Immunology, Neurology and in antibody and protein therapies (biologics)

Understanding the pharma CVC ecosystem Establish the background and explain how corporate venture investment has evolved

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Evolution of Biopharma Investment VC = Financial Return Driven: Focuses primarily on identifying high-growth startups and generating attractive investment returns CVC = Strategic + Financial Return Driven: Focuses on accessing external innovation, strengthening corporate pipelines, building strategic partnerships and identifying potential acquisition opportunities ~65% New molecular entity launches in 2023 were externally sourced; >70% of NME revenues since 2018 19% vs 9% Phase I-to-launch success: partnered vs non-partnered assets (2015-2022) 18 rounds Novo Holdings joined the most private venture rounds in 2025 (Lilly and Sanofi Ventures: 13 each) Evolution of the Funding Ecosystem Strategic Rationale for Pharma InvestmentExpanding Investor Participation Traditional VC-led model Seed, Series A-C and early clinical-stage funding of discovery to development Pharma enters via dedicated CVC arms Novo Holdings, Lilly and Sanofi lead venture-round activity; MSD’s $600M evergreen GHI Fund extends CVC into digital health Diversified capital ecosystem Private Equity, banks, asset managers, SWFs and crossovers join via co-investments and private rounds Key message: Financing is moving beyond VC toward strategic pharma capital combined with institutional financial investment. Corporate VC Strategic minority stakes and co-investments to access innovation and future partnerships Private Equity (PE) Growth and platform investments; long-term value creation and commercialization Investment Banks IPO underwriting and private placements; intermediaries, not direct investors Asset Managers Public equities, private funds and crossover positions for diversification and returns Sovereign Wealth Funds (SWF) Direct investments, fund commitments and co- investments for long-term returns Crossover Investors Pre-IPO private rounds to capture value before listing or acquisition Note: Banks facilitate financing; VC, PE, CVC and institutional investors may deploy direct capital. A B Pipeline Diversification New therapeutic areas and differentiated clinical assets; less reliance on internal candidates C Strategic Partnerships Co-development, licensing and research collaboration with shared R&D risk D Potential Acquisition Opportunities Early access and relationships ahead of future licensing or acquisition Access to Innovation Early exposure to novel targets, modalities and platforms hard to build internally Implication: Biotechs increasingly gain both financial capital and strategic capabilities from investors. External capital is becoming a strategic pharma tool, not just a source of funding, to secure innovation, improve pipeline productivity and build future dealmaking options. From Traditional VC to a Diversified Strategic Capital Ecosystem

Who is investing and where is the capital flowing? Showcase funding activity, leading rounds and the most active corporate investors

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Biopharma Financing Landscape (Jan 2025-Jul 2026) Biopharma Financing Trends: Biopharma Financing activity remains active, with 161 disclosed deals generating ~$14.5B in investment. Follow- on rounds lead on both capital (61% of dollars) and deal volume (53% of deals), while new financings account for 35% of deals and 27% of capital. Q2 2026 marked a quarterly peak, recording 35 deals and $3.5B invested 161 Disclosed deals Q2 2026 Peak: 35 deals, $3.5B ~$14.5B Total invested $90M Avg. deal | $75M median New vs follow-on financings 27% 61% 12% 35% 53% 12% $14.5B total 161 deals Share of investment ($) Share of deal count New (Seed, Series A): 57 deals, $4.0B Follow-on (B–E, PIPE): 85 deals, $8.8B Unspecified round: 19 deals, $1.7B Quarterly investment ($M) and disclosed deals 0 12 24 36 48 0 1,000 2,000 3,000 4,000 Q1 2025 Q2 2025 Q3 2025 Q4 2025 Q1 2026 Q2 2026 Q3 2026* New ($M) Follow-on ($M) Unspecified ($M) Disclosed deals (rhs) Deals per quarter Q1 2025 = 30 Q2 2025 = 20 Q3 2025 = 18 Q4 2025 = 25 Q1 2026 = 25 Q2 2026 = 35 Q3 2026* = 8 61% of capital Follow-on rounds took 61% of dollars from 53% of deals. Strengths & risks of the CVC model Assess what the CVC model offers pharma & where it carries risk

Positioning corporate venture capital for future innovation-led growth while navigating investment discipline, strategic alignment and evolving market risks S W • Access to external innovation: CVCs can provide corporations with early access to emerging technologies, startup capabilities and external R&D, strengthening long-term competitiveness • Strategic commercial synergies: Parent companies can leverage established distribution networks, industry expertise and customer relationships to support portfolio-company growth and commercialisation • Diversified innovation exposure: CVC helps companies get an early look at new technologies outside their main business. CVCs took part in 68% of AI investment value in 2025 and are moving into climate, defence, and manufacturing; In Q2 2026, they made 1,087 deals, with software and AI attracting the most money • Dependence on corporate priorities: Changes in leadership, strategic direction or internal budgets may disrupt investment continuity and weaken long-term CVC commitments • Difficulty measuring returns: Balancing strategic objectives, such as technology access and innovation, with financial performance may complicate investment evaluation • Corporate decision-making constraints: Complex approval structures and limited investment autonomy may slow deal execution and reduce competitiveness against independent venture capital firms • AI and emerging-technology investments: Growing corporate investment in AI, enterprise software and digital infrastructure could create opportunities to access transformative technologies and future business models • Strategic partnerships and acquisitions: CVC investments can create pathways for technology licensing, co-development, commercial partnerships and selective acquisitions of innovative startups • Expansion into emerging markets: Asia's significant share of global CVC deal activity presents opportunities to access new startup ecosystems, technologies and entrepreneurial talent O T • Competitive knowledge leakage: Co-investing with competing corporations may expose a CVC's proprietary technology insights, market intelligence and strategic priorities to potential industry rivals • Conflicting investment objectives: Multiple corporate investors may pursue different strategic goals, creating disagreements over technology access, commercial partnerships and future business opportunities • Reduced investment influence: When several corporate investors participate in the same startup, an individual CVC may have less influence over strategic decisions, governance and access to exclusive commercial opportunities • Co-investment coordination challenges: A growing number of investment partners can increase coordination complexity, create information-sharing challenges and reduce the effectiveness of collaboration Month: October 2026 Presenter: Team Octavus From an historically elusive target to a new frontier in precision oncology Insights Corner R EWRITING THE RULES OF AS INHIBITOR

AGENDA Content INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com RAS Targeting Fundamentals & Therapeutic Evolution 06 07 Clinical Development & Emerging Evidence Competitive Landscape & Clinical Benchmarking 11 16 Company Positioning & Investment Perspectives 21 Future Outlook & Strategic Opportunities 25 Executive Summary

For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Highlights from AACR-25 (May, 25) US Tariff impact on Pharma industries (Jun, 25) EULAR-25: Key insights of Psoriatic Arthritis (Jul, 25) Antibody Drug Conjugate: The next big investment in Oncology (Aug, 25) Animal Health (Oct, 25) Obesity deep dive (Nov, 25) GLP-1 and GIP (Dec, 25) Hematological Highlights from ASH 2025 (Jan, 26) China Biotech’s Global Positioning from JPM-26 (Feb,26) BIOSIMILARS RISING: The Catalyst For A New Age In Biologics Therapies (Mar,26) Cell Therapy Within CGT (Apr, 26) Gene Therapy Within CGT (May, 26) Regulatory Designations US FDA & EMA (June, 26) RadioTherapy Highlights (July, 26) AI in Drug Development (Aug, 26) Companion Diagnostic (Sep, 26) Additional: 1 Beautiful Bill PRIOR ISSUES INSIGHTS CORNER

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Executive Summary INSIGHTS CORNER RAS has moved from “undruggable” to a validated target: RAS alterations occur in ~30% of human cancers. After KRAS G12C inhibitors (sotorasib in 2021, adagrasib in 2022), the field has moved to broader RAS(ON) approaches; Daraxonrasib (RASONQUE) received FDA approval in Aug 2026 for previously treated metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma; New IV modalities such as the liposomal HRS-4642 and the protein degrader ARV-806 are emerging, though their clinical differentiation is not yet proven Clinical evidence is strong and development is accelerating: In P3 RASolute 302, daraxonrasib roughly doubled survival versus chemotherapy: mOS 13.2 vs 6.7 mos and mPFS 7.2 vs 3.6 mos, with ORR of 31.6% vs 11.2% in the overall population; Zoldonrasib + daraxonrasib showed ORRs of 50% (2L) and 47% (3L+) in KRAS G12D mPDAC. There are 13 ongoing trials in 2026, up from 1 in 2020; Early-stage studies dominate (52 of 79 trials are P1 or 1/2), and 12 trials were terminated The competitive race is shifting to earlier lines, G12D and combinations: Daraxonrasib now sets the benchmark. Divarasib beat sotorasib/adagrasib on PFS and OS in the P3 Krascendo 1 study; In contrast, the FDA withdrew the adagrasib + cetuximab accelerated approval in CRC after KRYSTAL-10 missed both primary endpoints; The G12D space is crowded with IV inhibitors, degraders and RAS(ON/OFF) drugs, and new entrants must now compete against an approved RAS(ON) inhibitor Revolution Medicines is the central value story: The FDA approval is the company’s first proprietary product- revenue stream, following zero reported revenue in FY2024 and FY2025; It has $3.9B in cash and investments as of Jun 30, 2026; Daraxonrasib peak revenue is forecast at $15.1B (2034), with a 2027 forecast of $2.4B and a 30-day supply priced at $39,800; Analysts are bullish: Morgan Stanley is Overweight with a $255 target, and JPMorgan raised its target from $227 to $246; The deck’s market-sizing illustration implies a roughly $30B opportunity (not a sales forecast), against an EV of nearly $15B Future leadership will depend on durability, safety and earlier-line use: The outlook centers on four themes: expansion beyond G12C (G12D, G12V, pan-RAS), rational combinations, earlier-line and new-indication use, and overcoming acquired resistance; Key upcoming catalysts include RASolve 301 initial results (NSCLC, 2H 27–1H 28 window), the Divarasib Krascendo 1 full results at ESMO, and P3 starts for several G12D and pan-RAS assets; Success will hinge on proven clinical benefit and regulatory approval, not early response rates alone

FOUNDATION RAS Targeting Fundamentals

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com THERAPEUTIC EVOLUTION RAS BIOLOGY1 WHY RAS IS AN IMPORTANT ONCOLOGY TARGET2 THERAPEUTIC RATIONALE3 4 RAS family: KRAS, NRAS and HRAS are small GTPases that act as molecular switches regulating cell proliferation, survival and differentiation. Normal signaling: RAS cycles between GDP-bound inactive (OFF) and GTP-bound active (ON) states following upstream growth-factor activation. Oncogenic activation: Mutations, predominantly at G12, G13 and Q61, can impair GTP hydrolysis and maintain RAS in an active state. Constitutively active RAS stimulates downstream RAF– MEK–ERK (MAPK) and PI3K-AKT signaling, promoting tumor growth and survival. RAS alterations occur in ~30% of human cancers, making the RAS pathway one of the most frequently altered oncogenic signaling systems. KRAS is the predominant mutated RAS isoform and is particularly prevalent in pancreatic, colorectal and non-small-cell lung cancers (NSCLC). Direct RAS inhibition was historically challenging because of the protein’s high affinity for GTP/GDP and lack of obvious drug-binding pockets, leading to its longstanding reputation as an “undruggable” target. RAS mutation → persistent RAS signaling → MAPK / PI3K pathway activation → tumor proliferation & survival Direct RAS inhibition Mutant RAS blockade → downstream signaling suppression → reduced tumor-cell growth Advances in structural biology and medicinal chemistry identified exploitable pockets in mutant RAS, enabling mutation-selective direct inhibitors. “Undruggable” RAS High affinity for GTP/GDP and lack of druggable pockets Direct KRAS Targeting Focus on inhibiting mutant RAS activity KRAS G12C Inhibitors First successful mutation- selective direct inhibitors Emerging RAS-Targeting Strategies G12D, G12V, G12R, G13D and pan-RAS approaches Clinical Impact Expanding treatment options & improving outcomes in RAS-driven cancers The first major clinical validation came with KRAS G12C inhibitors, beginning with sotorasib (2021) and followed by adagrasib (2022) in KRAS G12C- mutated NSCLC. Once considered “undruggable,” RAS has emerged as a major frontier in precision oncology. Advances in structure-guided drug design have enabled direct targeting of mutant RAS, from clinically validated KRAS G12C inhibitors to emerging strategies targeting additional RAS variants and broader RAS signaling. RAS Inhibitors: From Oncogenic Driver to Targeted Therapy

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com RAS first studied through rodent tumor viruses; human HRAS, KRAS and NRAS oncogenes identified. PERIOD Late 1960s-1983 MILESTONE WHY IT’S MATTER 1980s-1990s 1990s-2000s 2013 May 2021 Dec 2022 Jun 2024 Jan 2025 2020s-2026 Aug 2026 RAS GTPase biology and signaling partners including SOS, GAPs and RAF were characterized; RAS membrane localization and farnesylation became therapeutic targets. Farnesyltransferase inhibitors and downstream pathway inhibitors were explored clinically. A druggable pocket on KRAS G12C was identified, enabling covalent inhibitor development. Sotorasib received the first FDA approval of a KRAS-targeted therapy, for previously treated KRAS G12C-mutated NSCLC. Adagrasib received accelerated FDA approval for previously treated KRAS G12C-mutated NSCLC. Adagrasib + cetuximab received accelerated FDA approval for previously treated KRAS G12C-mutated colorectal cancer. Sotorasib + panitumumab received FDA approval for previously treated KRAS G12C- mutated metastatic colorectal cancer. RAS(ON) inhibitors and broader RAS-targeting strategies advanced beyond G12C- specific inhibition. Daraxonrasib (RASONQUE) received FDA approval for metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma after prior therapy or in patient's ineligible for multiagent systemic treatment. Established RAS as a cancer-driving gene family. Explained how RAS switches on growth signaling and why it was difficult to inhibit directly. Early approaches exposed limitations of indirectly targeting RAS, including alternative signaling and pathway feedback. Provided a practical route to directly inhibit a specific mutant RAS protein. First clinical proof that KRAS could be directly targeted with a medicine. Expanded the clinical options for KRAS G12C-driven disease. Demonstrated the importance of combination therapy in colorectal cancer. Established another approved KRAS G12C combination approach in colorectal cancer. The field began targeting multiple RAS mutants and expanding into cancers such as pancreatic cancer. A major milestone for broader RAS-family targeting beyond KRAS G12C. RAS inhibitor history reflects a shift from indirect pathway blockade to direct, mutation-selective targeting; approved KRAS G12C inhibitors established clinical proof of concept, while broader RAS-targeting approaches are expanding the landscape, with efficacy and durability remaining key challenges. RAS Inhibitors History: Decades of Discovery Reshaping the RAS Targeting Landscape

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com MILESTONE MOLECULE TARGET FORMULATION / ROUTE STATUS 2021 Sotorasib (LUMAKRAS) KRAS G12C Tablet/Oral FDA Approved 2022 Adagrasib (KRAZATI) KRAS G12C Tablet/Oral FDA Approved 2026 Daraxonrasib (RASONQUE) RAS(ON) multi- selective Tablet/Oral FDA Approved 1 2 3 4 OPPORTUNITY STRATEGIC RATIONALE Improve tumor exposure IV/liposomal delivery may increase delivery to tumor tissue Overcome oral bioavailability limitations Bypasses GI absorption Enable new modalities Protein degraders and other non-conventional RAS approaches may favor parenteral delivery Controlled PK Direct systemic delivery can support defined exposure and intermittent dosing Combination therapy IV RAS inhibitor can potentially be integrated into existing infusion-based oncology regimens Potential differentiation Formulation itself could become a differentiating attribute if linked to better exposure/efficacy MARKET ENTRY: ORAL WAS THE STARTING POINT Sotorasib became the first FDA-approved direct RAS-targeted therapy on May 28, 2021, as a once-daily oral tablet. Adagrasib followed in 2022, also as an oral tablet, so the first commercial RAS inhibitors were all oral small molecules. WHY THE FORMULATION LANDSCAPE MAY CHANGE A 2026 Cancer Cell review notes that the first-generation KRAS G12C inhibitors are limited by rapid emergence of resistance, while newer mechanisms and broader RAS coverage are being pursued. New RAS modalities may not have the same oral bioavailability characteristics Resistance remains major limitation of 1st-generation KRAS G12C inhibitors Potentially suboptimal tumor exposure GI tolerability / absorption challenges PROOF THAT IV RAS TARGETING IS ALREADY EMERGING HRS-4642 - KRAS G12D INHIBITOR IV LIPOSOMAL FORMULATION • Modality: selective KRAS G12D small-molecule inhibitor • Formulation: liposomal nanoparticle • Route: IV infusion • Clinical stage: Phase 1b/2 • Population: KRAS G12D-mutant pancreatic cancer ✓ Reported in 30 previously untreated patients: Confirmed ORR 63.3% (95% CI 43.9–80.1) ✓ RP2D: 500 mg Day 1 + 1,200 mg Day 8, every 3 weeks ✓ Phase 1b: Reported no dose-limiting toxicities Nature Medicine describes HRS-4642 as a liposomal nanoparticle given intravenously to improve tumor accumulation & prolong target inhibition. Earlier P1 data showed weekly, every-2-week and every-3- week IV schedules, supporting intermittent dosing. THE STRATEGIC TAKEAWAY ARV-806 - KRAS G12D PROTEIN DEGRADER • Target: KRAS G12D • Modality: Targeted protein degradation • Route: IV infusion • Development: Phase 1/2 first in human study • Clinical result: No clinical efficacy result posted in the trial record NCT07023731: ARV-806 is being administered through a vein (IV infusion) in a P1/2 study in KRAS G12D-mutant advanced solid tumors. Is there scope for IV RAS inhibitors? YES, but primarily for next- generation modalities Oral KRAS inhibitors established clinical proof of concept; emerging IV formulations and protein degraders are exploring alternative ways to deliver mutation-selective RAS targeting, with clinical benefit and differentiation still to be demonstrated. RAS Inhibitors: Beyond Oral Small Molecules to Emerging IV Modalities

EVIDENCE Clinical Development & Evidence

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com PHASE WISE STATUS WISE RAS Inhibitors: Comprehensive Analysis of Clinical Trial on RAS Mutation from 2020 to till now Not yet recruiting, 7, 9% Recruiting, 34, 43% Active, not recruiting, 9, 12% Completed, 11, 14% Enrolling by invitation, 1, 1% Terminated, 12, 15% Suspended, 1, 1% Unknown, 4, 5% AGE WISE YEAR WISE ONGOING TRIALs (Active Not Recruiting & Recruiting) 27 25 16 11 0 5 10 15 20 25 30 Phase 1 Phase 1/2 Phase 2 Phase 3 1 3 3 6 6 11 13 0 5 10 15 20 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026 2 79 79 0 20 40 60 80 100 Child Adult Older Adult INSIGHTS Development momentum is accelerating 13 ongoing trials in 2026 The highest annual count in the dataset, up from 1 in 2020, suggesting sustained clinical development momentum. Confirm whether 2026 represents a full year. Early-stage development dominates 52 trials Phase I and Phase I/II account for 52 of the 79 trials represented in the phase chart, indicating a substantial early-stage pipeline and a need to monitor progression toward later-stage evidence. Clinical attrition warrants attention 12 terminated trials Terminated studies represent 15% of the 79 trials in the status chart. Understanding termination reasons, efficacy signals, safety, and resistance mechanisms can help identify development risks. Broad Adult Eligibility 79 trials Each Adult and older-adult eligibility categories each appear in 79 entries, compared with just 2 in the child category. Because age groups may overlap within the same trial, these figures reflect eligibility coverage rather than distinct trials, highlighting the predominantly adult-focused scope of RAS inhibitor research. RAS inhibitor research is accelerating, but the real breakthroughs are yet to come. The next wave of late- phase results will decide which therapies redefine cancer treatment. Till date

Shift Toward Rational Combination Therapies Combining RAS inhibitors with EGFR, SHP2, SOS1, or downstream pathway inhibitors may improve response depth and durability. In colorectal cancer, EGFR co-inhibition is already an established strategy for KRAS G12C-targeted treatment. Overcoming Acquired Resistance Tumors can develop mutations or activate alternative pathways that reduce treatment effectiveness. Next-generation inhibitors, protein-degrading drugs, and biomarker-guided combination therapies may help overcome these resistance mechanisms. Earlier-Line Treatment & Indication Expansion Positive clinical trial results may enable RAS inhibitors to be used earlier in treatment and across more cancer types. Success will depend on proven efficacy, safety, and regulatory approval, not just early response rates. Oncology RAS inhibitors are evolving beyond KRAS G12C toward broader mutation coverage, rational combinations, and resistance management. Future competitive leadership will depend on durable efficacy, manageable safety, and proven clinical benefit, with successful trials potentially enabling earlier-line use and stronger market positioning. 4 2 3 G12D agents enter Ph 3: zoldonrasib + chemo 1L PDAC (RASolute 305); Incyte INCB161734 1L (DAWN-303). Jun 29, 2026FDA selects seven firms for a drug manufacturing pilot FDA selected seven companies for its PreCheck Pilot Program to strengthen US pharmaceutical manufacturing and supply-chain resilience: Amneal, Cellares, Eli Lilly, FUJIFILM Biotechnologies, Kriya Therapeutics, Kyowa Kirin, and Regeneron. The two-phase model offers early facility guidance and enhanced application support. Sep 21, 2026 FDA revises regulations to promote innovative alternatives to animal testing FDA rule: Clarifies that Non-Animal Methods (NAMs) can support safety assessments of drugs and biologics before human trials, where appropriate Expanded approaches: Recognizes human cells, organ-on-chip systems, and computational models, while replacing animal-focused terminology with “nonclinical” No new requirements: The rule does not prohibit animal studies, change evidentiary standards, or add new development requirements NAMs database & comments: FDA launched a 25-example NAMs use-case database and is accepting public comments; significant adverse comments could lead to withdrawal and standard rulemaking 6

UPDATES EU Based Updates This slide is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Jul 02, 2026 EMA advances efforts to address women’s health needs Sep 01, 2026 Voluntary Data Submission Pilot to Accelerate Alternatives to Animal Testing EMA launched a voluntary data submission pilot to facilitate the sharing and regulatory assessment of New Approach Methodologies (NAMs), including organoids, microphysiological systems, and computational models Purpose: Support the replacement or reduction of animal studies in medicines development Submission & feedback: Companies, researchers, and other stakeholders can submit NAM data independently of marketing applications and receive non-binding expert feedback Regulatory impact: The pilot aims to build regulatory experience, harmonise assessment approaches, and strengthen NAM acceptance across Europe Timeline: Submissions are expected through Q3 2027, followed by an EMA lessons-learned report Women’s health focus: EMA is integrating sex-specific considerations across medicines development and regulation Clinical & safety assessment: Focus includes trial representation, efficacy, safety, dosing, and pregnancy/breastfeeding evidence, alongside pharmacovigilance Evidence generation: EMA will expand DARWIN EU® real-world evidence studies, identify research gaps, and reduce regulatory uncertainty Collaboration & priorities: EMA will strengthen stakeholder and international collaboration, with the 28–29 September Women’s Health Workshop helping shape future priorities Data.lnsights.Decisions. 7

For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Executive Summary CDx is becoming integral to precision drug development, the FDA lists 168 biomarker-drug pairings linked to approved diagnostic tests, supporting biomarker-led patient selection, trial design, and treatment access The CDx market is expanding rapidly, projected in the deck to grow from $9.37B in 2026 to $28.75B by 2035, a 13.3% CAGR as targeted therapies and biomarker-defined populations increase Broader molecular profiling is replacing sequential single-marker testing, with NGS, comprehensive genomic profiling and multiplex platforms complementing traditional IHC, FISH and PCR to capture a wider range of actionable alterations CDx is expanding beyond one-time treatment selection toward continuous and more personalized decision-making, with liquid biopsy/MRD, resistance monitoring, AI-assisted diagnostics, spatial/multi-omic approaches and decentralized testing emerging as important next-generation applications Scale, partnerships and evidence are becoming key competitive differentiators, as high development costs, regulatory requirements, reimbursement and implementation complexity favor integrated pharma-diagnostic ecosystems and established platform players INSIGHTS CORNER

CDx Is Becoming a Strategic Pillar of Precision Medicine

Cardiovascular disease is now the fastest-growing indication, signaling diversification beyond oncology. KEY HIGHLIGHTS KEY INSIGHTS ❖ CDx is now a built-in requirement of drug development The FDA lists 168 biomarker-drug pairings linked to approved tests. Foundation Medicine hit 100 approved CDx indications across the US and Japan in December 2025. ❖ Liquid biopsy is the fastest-growing testing modality Tissue biopsy still leads by volume (77.95% in 2025), but liquid biopsy is growing at an 18.22% CAGR through 2031; Guardant360 CDx won FDA approval for this in September 2025 ❖ High costs are consolidating the field around established players Development can cost $50-100M and 3-5 years, pushing smaller firms into big-pharma alliances, reflected in Guardant Health’s ~$149M acquisition of MetaSight Diagnostics (Dec 2025) Market Landscape CDx Market size outlook (2025 – 2035)

• Broad NGS panels to analyse a large set of genes • Detects multiple alteration and genomic signatures, including TMB and MSI • Minimally invasive, detects tumour derived biomarkers in body fluids. • Alternative to conventional tissue biopsy • Integrates AI-driven digital pathology, spatial imaging, multi-omic data into diagnostic approach. • Predictive and personalized insights • Established patient selection for targeted therapies • Improved benefit–risk balance • Fast, interpretable, and accessible testing • Foundation of the CDx model • Enables longitudinal profiling • Detects acquired resistance • Supports approved blood based CDx use cases • Provides spatial and cellular context • Improves response and resistance understanding • Strengthens immuno-oncology biomarker assessment • Simultaneous testing of multiple predefined biomarkers • Shorter diagnostic pathway • Broader treatment option identification • Higher detection of actionable alterations • Enables more precise therapy matching • Supports rare biomarker detection • Longer turnaround time and higher cost • Complex interpretation • Uncertain findings may not translate into patient benefit • Risk of false negative or positive • Negative results may not exclude actionable alterations • Reduced sensitivity in early stage tumors • Complex sample preparation and data-analysis • Standardization challenges • Need for clinical validation, regulatory clarity, and reimbursement evidence. • Limited multiplexing capability • Reduced biomarker coverage • Dependence on tissue quality • Assay, scoring, and interpretation variability • Limited predefined gene and variant coverage • Risk of missing rare, novel, • alterations • Dependence on adequate tumor content • Sensitivity to nucleic-acid quality The Engine Behind Companion Diagnostic Next-generation technologies driving biomarker detection and treatment selection Abb: CDx: Companion diagnostic; CDx Ecosystem Is Becoming More Integrated: From Development to Commercialization

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Aug 2026: Oncology ISH Test Systems Reclassified to Class II Certain oncology ISH systems can transition from PMA to the 510(k) pathway with special controls, reducing regulatory burden for eligible tests. It aims to support innovation and improve patient access to oncology diagnostics, while special controls continue to ensure safety and effectiveness. Note: Effective from 16 Sep 2026 Nov 2025: Proposed Reclassification of Oncology Nucleic Acid-Based CDx FDA proposed a Class III-to-Class II shift for eligible oncology nucleic acid-based CDx, potentially enabling a faster 510(k)- based route to market. The aim is to facilitate development of these oncology diagnostics while maintaining appropriate safety and effectiveness controls. Aug 2026: CDx Consultation Procedure Update (Rev. 4): EMA updated CDx consultation guidance, clarifying IRIS submission, timelines, pre-submission engagement, and application requirements. The update directly supports how Notified Bodies and CDx manufacturers should navigate the EMA CDx consultation process. Dec 2025: MDR/IVDR Guidance for Medicinal Product-Device Combinations Updated EU guidance clarifies requirements for medicinal product and device combinations, including CDx consultation roles for EMA and national authorities. Mar 2025: CDx Classification Clarification (MDCG 2020-16 rev.4) CDx are classified under IVDR Rule 3(f) and must be linked to a medicinal product identified by INN. This classification determines the applicable conformity-assessment requirements and CDx consultation with EMA or national authorities. Dec 2024: Guidance on CDx Consultation Procedure EMA issued guidance on the procedural aspects of consultation between Notified Bodies and EMA for CDx. It provides practical guidance on the submission, consultation process, timelines and interactions between Notified Bodies and EMA when assessing CDx under the IVDR. Abb: CDx: Companion Diagnostic; ISH: In Situ Hybridization Test; IVD: In Vitro Diagnostic; IVDR: In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation; PMA: Premarket Approval US FDA EMA Risk based regulation Proportionate to diagnostic risk Streamlined pathways Potentially reducing time to market Better patient access To innovative oncology drugs CDx at a Regulatory Crossroads US FDA & EMA policy shifts shaping CDx development, 2024–2026 INSIGHTS CORNER

Adoption Still Depends on Solving Evidence, Access & Implementation Gaps

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com BIOMARKER DISCOVERY CLINICAL DEVELOPEMNT ASSAY VALIDATION REGULATORY APPROVAL REIMBURSEMENT & PATIENT ACCESS PATIENT TREATMENT Unmet NeedWhy it Matters? 1 2 34 5 PATIENT ACCESS & CLINICAL IMPACT Delays limit time to the right therapy Patient can be misclassified or miss treatment opportunities Inefficiencies increase cost and reduce system capacity Coordinated action across the ecosystem is needed Integrated drug– biomarker–CDx development from early clinical stages Interoperable assays, biomarker-level harmonization, and less invasive testing solutions Globally harmonized, technology-agnostic regulatory pathways Integrated drug + diagnostic market-access strategies and near-real- time testing infrastructure Shared-value partnership models and platform- based CDx lifecycle strategies Development & Evidence Assay Harmonization & Sample Access Regulatory & Technology Complexity Reimbursement & Diagnostic Access Ecosystem & Lifecycle Management Biomarker and CDx strategies are often finalized late; clinical trial assays may differ from commercial tests, requiring bridging studies Multiple tests for the same biomarker, inconsistent cutoffs, tissue scarcity, tumor heterogeneity, and biopsy burden can lead to patient misclassification Divergent global regulatory requirements and emerging technologies such as NGS, ctDNA, AI pathology, and multi-omics challenge traditional CDx frameworks Regulatory approval does not guarantee reimbursement, laboratory availability, or timely testing; turnaround time can delay treatment decisions Diagnostic developers bear significant R&D and regulatory costs but may capture limited value from successful therapies; CDx requirements evolve as drugs gain new indications CUMULATIVE DELAYS ACROSS THE CDx ECOSYSTEM The CDx Readiness Gap: Challenges Across the Patient Journey Five strategic barriers limiting the development, adoption, and real-world impact of CDx

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Testing Uptake Remains Uneven Coverage and Reimbursement are Critical Gatekeepers CDx in Europe: Reimbursement Gaps Limit Patient Access ❖ Unequal insurance coverage continues to limit access to genomic testing ❖ Before CMS introduced NCD, regional MACs made genomic testing coverage decisions through LCDs, resulting in regional variations in coverage and access ❖ Access to testing is influenced by clinical guidelines, physician awareness, tissue availability, and certified laboratory ❖ “Enhancing CLIA Act 2026” proposed that LDTs with supplemental 3rd party affirmation be treated as equivalent to US FDA-approved tests for NCDs & use as CDx ❖ Medicare’s NCD standardized national coverage policies, reduced administrative uncertainty, and supported wider adoption of NGS testing ❖ Potentially extending the proposed NCD equivalence framework to recognize supplemental-affirmed LDTs as equivalent to US FDA-approved assays under LCDs ❖ In many European countries, reimbursed cancer drug may still lack coverage for its associated CDx, limiting timely patient access to treatment ❖ Sequential drug approval, CDx certification, and national reimbursement decisions can extend timelines and create additional barriers to market access ❖ Differences in diagnostic infrastructure and reimbursement systems create disparities in CDx testing access between countries What Drives Payer Coverage? Evidences Assessment Framework Strategic Implications for CDx Developers Design for Reimbursement Early Generate payer-relevant evidence alongside regulatory development rather than after approval Demonstrate Clinical Utility Evidence should show how testing changes treatment decisions and improves patient outcomes Build an Access Ecosystem Partnerships with laboratories, healthcare systems, oncologists, and payers are essential for adoption Plan for Evolving Indications As CDx support additional drugs or indications, reimbursement policies and evidence requirements may need to evolve Clinical Evidence • Analytical validity • Clinical validity • Clinical utility • Impact on treatment decisions & patient outcomes Economic Evidence • Cost-effectiveness • Budget impact • Avoided unnecessary treatment • Healthcare resource utilization Implementation Evidence • Laboratory readiness • Testing turnaround time • Physician adoption • Integration into clinical workflows Abb: CDx: Companion Diagnostic; CMS: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services; LCD: Local Coverage Determination; LDTs: Laboratory-Developed Tests; MACs: Medicare Administrative Contractors; NCD: National Coverage Determination Market Access & Reimbursement of CDx From Regulatory Approval to Real-World Patient Access

For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com 1 2 3 4 FoundationOne CDx: Beyond US FDA Approval-Success or Stall? Market access depends on regulatory validation, clinical utility, and payer-recognized medical necessity Success: From US FDA Approval to Reimbursed Access Friction: US FDA Approval does not Guarantee Payment Real-world Denial Examples REGULATORY VALIDATION FoundationOne CDx US FDA-authorized NGS based test US FDA Approval: Nov 30, 2017 PMA: P170019 US FDA – CMS Parallel Review Coordinated approval & coverage assessment Accelerated access to innovative medical technologies for Medicare patients CMS National Coverage Pathway Improved Precision Oncology Access CMS covers FDA- approved/cleared Coverage applies when used for labeled cancer indications to guide patient management Reduced reimbursement uncertainty & delay Broader access to clinically actionable genomic testing NATIONAL MEDICAL COVERAGE PATIENT ACCESS COORDINATED COVERAGE PATHWAY Coordinated regulatory and coverage planning translated diagnostic innovation into a defined reimbursement pathway Abb: CDx: Companion Diagnostic; CMS: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services; PMA: Premarket Approval REGULATORY APPROVAL PAYER-LEVEL COVERAGE COMMERCIAL ADOPTION FoundationOne CDx US FDA-authorized CDx across multiple oncology indications Biomarker oncology linked to treatment selection CMS / Commercial Payers US FDA approval does not guarantee payment in every case Individual claims can face medical- necessity denials Coverage remains indication & payer dependent Routine Testing & Patient Access Guideline (NCCN, ASCO) support may facilitate ordering Adoption can still depend on payer coverage breadth New York External Appeal (2022) Highmark (2022) A health plan denied FoundationOne CDx for NSCLC patients despite NCCN support & reimbursement; insurer cited the broad 324-gene panel as not medically appropriate. Denial upheld FoundationOne CDx was denied for the lung-cancer patients; payer considered NGS testing exceeding>50 genes not medical necessary. Denial upheld. Regulatory approval establishes CDx eligibility-but payer recognized clinical utility & medical necessity determine coverage 1 2 3 US FDA approval opens the reimbursement pathway; sustained access depends on payer acceptance of clinical utility and medical necessity

item.title: Octavus Insights Corner - AI in Drug Development (August 2026)
item.description: Octavus Insights Corner for August 2026: AI in drug development.
item.content:encoded:
Month: August 2026 Presenter: Team Octavus RUG EVELOPMENTD Insights Corner AI IN

AGENDA Content INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com From Data to Discovery: The AI foundation of drug development 04 05 AI Governance: From rules to readiness From Innovation to Value: Mapping the AI Opportunity 09 12 From Innovation to Clinical Impact 14 From Competitive Signals to Strategic Advantage 17 Executive Summary The Road Ahead: The next frontier of AI in drug development 22

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Highlights from AACR-25 (May, 25) US Tariff impact on Pharma industries (Jun, 25) EULAR-25: Key insights of Psoriatic Arthritis (Jul, 25) Antibody Drug Conjugate: The next big investment in Oncology (Aug, 25) Animal Health (Oct, 25) Obesity deep dive (Nov, 25) GLP-1 and GIP (Dec, 25) Hematological Highlights from ASH 2025 (Jan, 26) China Biotech’s Global Positioning from JPM-26 (Feb,26) BIOSIMILARS RISING: The Catalyst For A New Age In Biologics Therapies (Mar,26) Cell Therapy Within CGT (Apr, 26) Gene Therapy Within CGT (May, 26) Regulatory Designations US FDA & EMA (June, 26) Radiotherapy (July,26) Additional: 1 Beautiful Bill PRIOR ISSUES INSIGHTS CORNER

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com 1 2 3 4 5 A Maturing Market, Not Yet Consolidated AI in drug development is projected to grow from ~$6.5B (2026) to ~$35.5B by 2035 at ~20.7% CAGR, but the market remains scattered. The top 5 vendors hold just ~11.8% share Clinical Validation Is Emerging AI-designed candidates are reaching late-stage trials: Insilico's rentosertib moved from target to preclinical candidate in 18 months and is now in Ph 3 in China with Breakthrough Therapy Designation Capital Concentrates in Oncology 29.2B has been invested across 437 deals since 2021, led by oncology (177 deals), while Novartis, Bayer, and Daiichi Sankyo now deploy AI internally across discovery, safety, and trial design Regulators Are Building the Rulebook FDA and EMA jointly issued 10 Good AI Practice principles (Jan 2026), and FDA's new 7- step AI credibility framework signals governance is becoming a market-entry requirement Integration Will Define the Winners Advantage will favor players who combine proprietary data, validated models, and regulatory-ready governance across the full lifecycle, not point-solution algorithms alone Executive Summary AI is shifting from an experimental tool to a regulator-recognized layer of drug development, with success hinging on validated data, governance, and clinical proof INSIGHTS CORNER

From Data to Discovery: The AI foundation of drug development Objective: Establish a fundamental understanding of AI, its role across the drug-development lifecycle, and its potential to accelerate development

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Introduction AI’s value is not simply speed, it is improving the quality and timing of development decisions • AI in drug development refers to using advanced computational models to analyze complex data and support faster, smarter decisions across target discovery, molecule design, clinical development, and post-market monitoring • AI enables data-driven decision-making across the drug-development lifecycle, from target identification to post-market monitoring • AI integrates complex datasets to prioritize candidates, optimize clinical trials, improve patient selection, and reduce development risks • Beyond accelerating timelines, AI can improve decision quality and resource efficiency, supported by robust data, validation, clinical oversight, and regulatory governance Machine Learning Advanced Analytics Deep Learning Generative AI Where AI is transforming the lifecycle Discovery Preclinical Clinical Regulatory Commercial AI acts across the pipeline, not a single point tool, but a connected layer of intelligence. Why it matters Faster Development Accelerated timelines Higher Success Probability Reduced attrition risk Lower R&D Costs Efficient resource use Smarter Decisions Data-driven insight

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com TARGET Biological Data & Scientific Knowledge: AI integrates human genetics, single-cell and molecular data with published literature to prioritize disease- relevant targets Evidence: Novartis used AI to analyze literature, human genetics and millions of single-cell experiments, identifying five ADPKD targets for further study DISCOVER AI-Powered Molecule Design & Screening: Designs new molecules, predicts key properties and prioritizes the most promising compounds for laboratory testing Evidence: Novartis used generative AI to design 15M potential compounds and evaluated ~60 in the laboratory in a molecular-glue project PRE-CLINICAL AI Safety & ADMET Prediction: Predicts toxicity, metabolic properties and other safety risks to prioritize experimental testing Evidence: Novartis used AI-generated cardiac activity profiles to predict potential cardiac toxicity, then validated the predictions in the laboratory CLINICAL AI-Enabled Trial Design & Patient Selection: Stratifies patients, predicts treatment response and optimizes trial design/site selection using clinical and multi-omics data Evidence: Daiichi Sankyo and Tempus are developing multimodal AI models to optimize patient selection and map treatment response for an oncology ADC program REGULATORY AI-Assisted Regulatory Evidence: Produces and analyses information supporting regulatory decisions on drug safety, effectiveness and quality Regulatory signal: FDA issued draft guidance in 2025; FDA and EMA jointly developed 10 Good AI Practice principles in 2026 POST-MARKET AI-Enabled Pharmacovigilance: Uses AI and machine learning to analyze real-world safety data and identify potential adverse-event signals Evidence: Bayer’s ML-based AE detection engine analyses high-volume, multi-channel safety reports to identify possible AEs and support pharmacovigilance reporting Disease Insight & Target Prioritization Scalable Design & Faster Prioritization Earlier Candidate Prioritisation Improved Trial Efficiency Evidence-processing Efficiency Faster & Scalable Surveillance AI is becoming a cross-functional decision-support layer across drug development, from target selection and molecule design to clinical development and post- market safety. Its near-term value lies in faster evidence analysis, broader data integration and more efficient R&D execution. AI Across Drug Development From data to decisions across the drug-development lifecycle

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Drug Development: The Traditional Path vs. the AI- Accelerated Journey AI is reshaping the entire drug development lifecycle; accelerating timelines, enabling smarter decisions, and improving patient outcomes Traditional drug development lifecycle 10-15+ years High cost High risk DISCOVERY PRECLINICAL CLINICAL DEVELOPMENT REGULATORY REVIEW COMMERCIALIZATION 2-4 YEARS ONGOING1-2 YEARS 6-7 YEARS 1-2 YEARS AI-enabled accelerated drug development lifecycle 6-9 years Lower cost Higher success DISCOVERY PRECLINICAL CLINICAL DEVELOPMENT REGULATORY REVIEW COMMERCIALIZATION 1-2 YEARS ONGOING6-12 MONTHS 3-5 YEARS 6-12 MONTHS

AI Governance: From rules to readiness Objective: Highlight the evolving regulatory framework and governance expectations for AI use across drug development

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Human-centric & Ethical Ai Risk-based Validation Compliance With Standards Clear Purpose & Governance Robust Development & Monitoring Guiding Principles for AI in Drug Development AI Across The Medicinal Product Life Cycle Drug Discovery Non-clinical Research Manufacturing Regulatory Submissions Pharmacovigilance Key Workplan Priorities (2026-2028) AI Literacy Training For Regulators Expansion of Darwin EU RWD Network Alignment With The EU AI Act Greater Use Of RWE & Advanced Data Analytics International Collaboration EMA-FDA Good AI Practice Principles in Drug Development (2026) EMA Reflection Paper on AI in the Medicinal Product Lifecycle Upcoming Regulation: EMA-HMA NDSG Workplan 2026-2028 A B C AI is being utilized more in drug development, requiring uniform regulatory oversight to ensure its safe, reliable, and transparent use for patient protection. Establishes common principles for the responsible AI development promoting risk-based validation, data quality, transparency, and international harmonization. On 14 Jan 2026, EMA and FDA jointly published 10 Good AI Practice (GAIP) principles for the medicine's life cycle, establishing a shared EU-US foundation for future AI guidance and regulatory use of AI-generated evidence WHY THIS IS IMPLEMENTED? PURPOSE OF THIS IMPLEMENT? CURRENT UPDATES ON THIS ? WHY THIS IS IMPLEMENTED? PURPOSE OF THIS IMPLEMENT? CURRENT UPDATES ON THIS ? Provides a framework for safe, responsible AI use in drug development, emphasizing reliability, transparency, scientific validity, and human oversight while addressing key risks such as bias, data quality, and cybersecurity. Guides pharmaceutical companies and regulators on the responsible use of AI throughout the medicinal product lifecycle, emphasizing human oversight, fit- for-purpose validation, and a clearly defined Context of Use (CoU). EMA’s active Reflection Paper sets risk-based expectations for responsible AI/ML use across the full medicines' lifecycle from discovery to post-authorisation. EMA is advancing its AI Strategy and Workplan, with the Reflection Paper serving as the scientific foundation. WHY THIS IS IMPLEMENTED? PURPOSE OF THIS IMPLEMENT? CURRENT UPDATES ON THIS ? The EMA and Heads of Medicines Agencies (HMA) introduced the updated Network Data Steering Group (NDSG) Workplan 2026- 2028 to establish a coordinated approach to data, AI, and RWE across the EU medicines regulatory network Strengthen evidence generation, regulatory efficiency and decision- making for trusted human and veterinary medicines The NDSG’s updated Workplan (February 2026) is being implemented through 2028, with priorities including EU AI Act, advanced analytics, Data Analysis and Real-World Interrogation Network (DARWIN EU 2), AI guidance for clinical development, pharmacovigilance, data standards and international collaboration Regulating AI in Healthcare in Drug Development EMA-FDA principles, reflection paper & upcoming regulations (2026-28)

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Considerations for the Use of Artificial Intelligence To Support Regulatory Decision-Making for Drug and Biological Products Draft guidance, January 2025A B Using Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning in the Development of Drug and Biological Products Discussion Paper, Revised February 2025 AI is increasingly being used in drug development, so FDA wants AI-generated evidence to be credible, transparent, and reliable. WHY THIS IS IMPLEMENTED? To provide a risk-based, 7-step framework for establishing and documenting the credibility of AI model outputs for a specific regulatory context of use PURPOSE OF THIS IMPLEMENT? Issued as draft guidance in January 2025, it recommends risk- proportionate assessment, lifecycle maintenance to address data drift, and early FDA engagement on the AI model, context of use, and credibility plan CURRENT UPDATES ON THIS ? AI is rapidly expanding in drug development, so FDA issued this discussion paper to understand the opportunities, challenges, and regulatory needs before developing formal guidance. WHY THIS IS IMPLEMENTED? To collect stakeholder feedback on the responsible use of AI/ML in drug development and help shape future FDA guidance and policies. PURPOSE OF THIS IMPLEMENT? CURRENT UPDATES ON THIS ? The FDA's core guidance sets a risk-based framework with a 7-step AI credibility assessment, while its companion paper gathers stakeholder feedback to shape future AI/ML policy. Together, they aim to ensure AI use in drug development is credible, transparent, and well-governed. KEY TAKEAWAYS FDA’s Evolving AI Regulatory Landscape Overview of key documents, purpose, and current update The February 2025 revised discussion paper outlines AI/ML applications across discovery, clinical research, safety surveillance, and manufacturing, while seeking stakeholder feedback on data quality, reliability, model validation, monitoring, and lifecycle management

From Innovation to Value: Mapping the AI Opportunity Objective: Assess market growth, adoption, competitive dynamics, and investment activity shaping AI in drug development

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com 6.5 7.9 9.5 11.5 13.9 16.7 20.2 24.4 29.4 35.5 2026 2027 2028 2029 2030 2031 2032 2033 2034 2035 MARKET SIZE ($B) $35.5B Projected market size by 2035 20.7% Asia-Pacific CAGR, 2026 - 2035 Fastest growing region, 2026 - 2035 ❖ Growth Drivers Oncology is the largest therapeutic area. North America leads on R&D spend; Asia-Pacific is the fastest-growing region ❖ Pharma/biotech remain the principal customers Pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies are identified as leading end users across several market studies ❖ Application leadership varies by definition Optimization/repurposing leads in some studies, while others identify de novo design or molecular-library screening as the largest application KEY HIGHLIGHTS KEY INSIGHTS ❖ Software-led, but not uniform Software accounts for ~62-68% of the market in selected studies; however, the software services mix varies with market scope and definition ❖ Provider landscape remains fragmented The supplier base spans specialized AI software, services and discovery platforms. The five leading vendors (Isomorphic Labs, Insitro, Insilico Medicine, Recursion and Schrodinger) collectively account for only ~11.8% of market share in one market assessment, indicating low market concentration ❖ Data and validation remain key constraints Data fragmentation/interoperability, model interpretability, validation and cross-disciplinary talent remain important adoption challenges Market Landscape AI in drug development: Market size outlook, 2025-2035

From Innovation to Clinical Impact Objective: Evaluate AI-enabled innovation, clinical validation, emerging technologies, and the evolving drug- development model

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com The convergence of AI, quantum capabilities, and specialized hardware has transformed drug discovery from brute-force laboratory screening into targeted computational simulation. Generative AI Systems & Software Quantum Computing Hardware & Hybrid Platforms Edge Computing & Smart Lab Systems Foundation Models for Biology: Domain- specific biological foundation models, such as Evo (Arc Institute) and AlphaFold 3 (DeepMind) For generate novel DNA/protein sequences Predicting biomolecular structures with ligands & nucleic acids For desiring de novo small molecules fitted to target binding pockets Cutting screening time from years to delay Diffusion & Generative AI: Tools like DiffDock and RFdiffusion design molecules for target binding, accelerating drug discovery. IBM Quantum and IonQ, integrated with cloud platforms, use VQE to model complex electronic structures beyond classical computing. Quantum-Classical Hybrid Cloud Infrastructure Quantum generative models can use fewer parameters than classical networks to generate more diverse, chemically accurate lead candidates. Quantum Generative AI (qGANs) Ibm Quantum IonQ Aws Bracket Azure Quantum Hybrid VQE Algorithm Experimental Quantum Process Models Fewer Parameters than Classical Networks More Diverse Chemically Accurate Lead Structures High-Throughput Edge AI Hardware: Specialized edge AI accelerators (Nvidia Jetson, Google Coral) integrated directly into laboratory hardware such as Automated High-Throughput Screening (HTS) rigs and Cryo-Electron Microscopes (Cryo-EM) process raw spatial data locally. Real-time Closed-loop Robotics: Edge nodes analyze real-time imaging or bio-assay outputs instantly to instruct robotic pipetting stations on next-step experiments without high-latency cloud roundtrips. AI Tech Trends in Drug Development

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Case Study: An End-to-End AI-Powered Drug Development Journey Rentosertib (INS018-055/ISM001-055) is an investigational oral TNIK inhibitor for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), discovered and designed by Insilico Medicine using its AI-powered Pharma.AI platform, including PandaOmics for target discovery and Chemistry42 for generative drug design 18 Months Target discovery to preclinical candidate (PandaOmics + Chemistry42) Year Development milestone AI platform used How AI contributed 2019 Analyzed IPF/fibrosis data and identified TNIK as a potential antifibrotic drug target PandaOmics within Pharma.AI PandaOmics analyzed IPF multi-omics, biological networks and scientific literature, ranking TNIK as the leading kinase target 2020 Generated and optimized novel TNIK inhibitors for potency, selectivity and drug-like properties Chemistry42 within Pharma.AI Chemistry42 used generative AI and predictive models to design TNIK inhibitors optimized for activity, ADME, solubility, stability and synthetic feasibility 2021 Final preclinical candidate nominated: INS018_055, later named rentosertib Pharma.AI: PandaOmics + Chemistry42 PandaOmics identified TNIK, while Chemistry42 designed and optimized the molecule; 79 compounds were synthesized and tested, leading to candidate nomination within ~18 months 2023- 24 Ph 2a was completed at 21 Chinese sites, enrolling 71 patients across placebo and three rentosertib dose groups PandaOmics supported exploratory biomarker analysis PandaOmics analyzed gene-expression data and fibrosis biomarkers 2025 China CDE Breakthrough Therapy Designation (May); Ph 2a results published in Nature Medicine (June) PandaOmics used for biomarker/context analysis PandaOmics supported gene-expression and biomarker analyses to contextualize fibrosis biology 2019 PandaOmics flags TNIK from IPF multi-omics data 2021 • Candidate nominated: INS018_055 • Ph 0 intiated microdose study (Australia) 2022-23 Ph 1 completed and received ODD from US FDA 2023-24 Ph 2a GENESIS-IPF completed in 21 sites of China 2025 Received BTD from China 2026 Ph 3 initiated in China

From Competitive Signals to Strategic Advantage Objective: Map the competitive landscape, technology capabilities, funding activity, and strategic implications for AI-enabled drug development

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com AI in Drug Discovery & Development AI is evolving beyond drug discovery to enable the entire pharma value chain from target identification and development to clinical trials and operations. The leading players differentiate through proprietary data, real world experimental validation, and deep integration into clinical and operational workflows. Discovery (AI developed small molecules drugs) Discovery (AI developed biological drugs) Preclinical development Clinical development Clinical documentation solutions Supply Chain management Software Platforms AI in Drug Development: The big picture From Discovery to Delivery: Mapping the AI innovators

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com AI-enabled drug discovery requires hybrid “TechBio” talent, quantum expertise, and strong AI validation capabilities. Success depends on FAIR data, automated labs, real-time feedback, and robust regulatory compliance. KEY TAKEAWAYS HUMAN SKILL TRANSFORMATION ENTERPRISE & STRUCTURAL READINESS The traditional boundary between bench wet-lab scientists and dry-lab computational chemists has collapsed. Organizations prioritize professionals proficient in both molecular biology/medicinal chemistry and Python, PyTorch, or Jax. Rise of the “TechBio” Scientist Biopharma computational teams are upskilling in quantum software development kits (e.g., Qiskit, PennyLane) to prepare classical datasets for hybrid quantum workflows. Quantum Chemistry Programming Teams are developing capabilities to audit generative models for biological feasibility, synthesizability, and toxico-genomic risks, moving past treat-as-black-box approaches. AI Model Validation Capability Large pharmaceutical firms are restructuring legacy clinical and multi-omics databases into standardized, machine-readable formats. FAIR Data Operations Structural readiness increasingly means connecting generative AI software directly to automated synthesis units via edge architectures. Self-Driving Labs (Lab Automation) Companies are establishing internal safety protocols to align with evolving regulatory frameworks (such as FDA guidelines on AI/ML-based drug development) to ensure full trace-and-audit capability for AI-generated drug candidates. Regulatory Compliance Frameworks Without clean, internal data, generative models produce hallucinated or non-synthesizable candidates. Ensure safety, traceability, and auditability from model to molecule. FAIR Data Foundation Automated Lab (Execute) Real-time Data (Feedback) Generative AI (Design) AI proposes compounds Automated liquid handlers synthesize Automated assays test in real-time Results refine generative algorithm Capability Trends in AI-Enabled Drug Development

The Road Ahead: The next frontier of AI in drug development Objective: The key trends and strategic shifts expected to shape the next phase of AI adoption across the drug development lifecycle

Better evidence-based target selection and more informed decisions. Faster iteration, higher productivity, and deeper exploration. Broader impact across the entire drug- development lifecycle. Competitive advantage comes from combining AI, data, and expertise. Validated models, strong governance, and transparent workflows drive scalable adoption. AI will accelerate target and drug candidate discovery. It will prioritize high- potential candidates using AI-driven biological insights. AI will integrate multi-omics, structural, chemical, and clinical data. This will enable a more comprehensive view of disease biology and drug discovery. AI, robotics, and automation will enable a continuous Design → Test → Learn → Redesign cycle. This will accelerate experimentation and optimize drug candidates more efficiently. AI will expand across the drug-development lifecycle, from preclinical research to post-market safety. Regulators are establishing frameworks for responsible, risk-based AI adoption. AI will augment not replace scientists by handling data analysis, prediction, & repetitive tasks. Scientists will drive biological interpretation, experimentation, & strategic decisions. AI adoption will shift from benchmark performance to real-world drug-development impact. Focus will be on clinical translation, better decisions, and responsible AI frameworks.
