INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com INSIGHTS CORNER Radiopharmaceuticals are shifting from a niche modality to a strategic oncology growth engine with success hinged on capacity, supply, and integration 1 2 3 4 5 A Mainstream Oncology Platform No longer a niche modality, Radiopharma is a core oncology growth engine, projected to grow from ~$7.9B (2026) to ~$17B (2035) at ~8.9% CAGR Theranostics Drives Adoption The “see it, treat it” model pairs imaging with matched therapy on one biomarker (led by Novartis LUTATHERA), and is expanding beyond PSMA/NETs into Fibroblast Activation Protein, Carbonic anhydrase IX, and GPCR targets Supply Becomes the Competitive Advantage Isotope production is concentrated in a handful of reactors, and alpha-emitter capacity lags projected demand, making supply security a true competitive barrier Policy and Capital Align Active US FDA/EMA guidance alongside more than $13B in deals since 2023 signal that regulators and investors are both moving to accelerate commercialization Integration Defines Winners With just-in-time supply chains, limited treatment-center capacity, and complex reimbursement, advantage will favour players who vertically integrate manufacturing, logistics, and care networks (e.g. ITM's Lu-177 supply + ITM-11 pipeline) Executive Summary

Foundations of Radiopharmaceuticals Objective: Establish a fundamental understanding of radiopharmaceuticals, theranostics, and their role in precision medicine

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Radiopharmaceuticals: Foundational Concepts Overview, mechanism of action and clinical applications of radiopharmaceuticals Overview According to WHO and IAEA, Radiopharmaceuticals are specialized medicinal formulations that contain radioisotopes and are used for the diagnosis and treatment of diseases across a wide range of clinical applications Abb: IAEA: International Atomic Energy Agency ; MPI: Myocardial Perfusion Imaging; PET: Positron Emission Tomography; WHO: World Health Organization Radiopharmaceuticals enable accurate delivery of radionuclides (radioactive isotope) linked to a vector (non- radioactive element) such as small molecules, peptides, and antibodies that target specific cells, tissues or organs in the body The Science behind Radiopharmaceuticals Radionuclide (Radioactive Isotope) Vector (Non-radioactive Element) Targeted Delivery (to specific cells, tissues & organs) Key Radioisotopes in clinical use Tc 99m F 18 I 131 Lu 177 used in a multiple diagnostic scans such as bone scans, kidney function tests and MPI used in PET imaging to diagnose cancer used to treat thyroid cancer used to treat neuroendocrine tumours Technetium -99m Fluorine-18 Iodine-131 Lutetium- 177

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com One Target Diagnostic and Therapeutic agents bind to the same biomarker for a unified approach Personalized care Imaging defines target expression and disease biology, guiding personalized therapy decisions Real-Time Assessment Enable assessment of disease activity and therapeutic response to guide ongoing patient care Better Outcomes Facilitate more targeted and efficient treatment approach, reducing adverse effects and improving clinical outcomes From Separate Pathways to Integrated Care Traditional Approach Conventional cancer treatment often involves distinct diagnostic and treatment processes. potentially resulting in treatment delays and a more complex patient journey More delays, Greater complexity A Growing Global Impact Oncology reviews describe an “exponential, global expansion” of radiotheranostics driven by its ability to target and eliminate tumor cells with relatively limited off target toxicity ESMO and other expert now present radioligand therapy (RLT) as a promising and increasingly relevant modality for the treatment of advanced & refractory cancers Radiotheranostic Approach Radiotheranostic integrates a diagnostic and a therapeutic radiopharmaceutical that act on same biomarker for simultaneous detection and treatment of diseases for more precise & efficient deliveryOne Target, Two solutions The Radiotheranostic Pathway Diagnostics Radiopharmaceuticals Therapeutics Radiopharmaceuticals Perform imaging to assess patient eligibility for the therapeutic agent Deliver targeted radiation to the same cancer cell targets selectively treating the disease “see it, treat it” Patient centered approach Theranostics: Bridging Diagnosis and Therapy Understanding the integration of molecular imaging and targeted radionuclide therapy to support precision medicine

Regulatory & Company Landscape Objective: Highlight the evolving regulatory environment and showcase Novartis leadership in advancing radioligand therapy

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com This guidance helps sponsors determine the optimal dosing regimen including administered activity and treatment schedule for oncology radiopharmaceutical therapies (RPTs) during clinical development before submitting a marketing application for a new indication. Note: It does not cover the selection of the initial administered activity for first-in-human RPTs trials or other aspects of RPTs clinical development, such as dosimetry software, fixed versus personalized dosimetry-based dosing, and theranostic co-development. This concept paper aims to identify aspects unique to therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals (tRPs) that should be addressed in a future guideline, complementing the existing “EMA Guideline on the Clinical Evaluation of Anticancer Medicinal Products”. The proposed guideline will provide specific recommendations on applying relevant regulatory principles to the clinical development of tRPs for marketing authorization applications. This guideline outlines the additional chemical, pharmaceutical, and biological information required for radiopharmaceuticals based on synthetic chemical substances when submitting marketing authorization applications or variations to authorized medicinal products. Dec 2025 (Draft) Aug 2025 (Draft) Oct 2024 Regulatory Landscape of Radiopharmaceuticals (2024-2026) Recent guidance, policy updates, and regulatory initiatives from the US FDA and EMA Guidelines for the quality of radiopharmaceuticals Dosage optimization for therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals in oncology during clinical development Concept paper on the clinical evaluation of therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals in oncology

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Revenue (2025): $54.5B Headquarter: Basel, Switzerland Business: Innovative medicines Therapeutic Focus: CVRM; Immunology; Neuroscience; Oncology Strategic Oncology Platform: Radioligand Therapy (RLT) Asset Indication Target ROA Planned filling dates Phase mHSPC - Registration Oligometastatic prostate cancer ≥2029 Phase 3 mCRPC; 1L ≥2029 Phase 3 post Lu mCRPC 2028 Phase 3 GEP NET 2028 Phase 3 AAA617 AAA617 AAA817 AAA817 AAA601 ▪ Novartis is consolidating leadership in RLT, with focused late-stage assets around SSTR and PSMA that deepen its control of GEP NET and prostate cancer segments ▪ Strong and growing RLT revenues (PLUVICTO, LUTATHERA) indicate RLT is now a core growth driver, enabling further investment that could entrench Novartis’ therapies as standards of care in these indications SSTR PSMA IV Infusion Approved Products Target Radioisotopes Approved Indication (Across US & EU) Revenue (Q1’26) $M SSTR lutetium 177 SSTR-positive GEP NET 211 PSMA lutetium 177 PSMA-positive mCRPC 642 Overview Clinical Pipeline (Phase 3 & Registration) 51,626 50,545 45,440 50,317 54,532 0 10,000 20,000 30,000 40,000 50,000 60,000 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 Financials FY Revenue ($M) Octavus Insight Patent Protection Products LUTATHERA 2029 (ODE expired) 2029 PLUVICTO 2034 2037 US EU NOVARTIS: Global Leader in Radioligand Therapy Exploring Novartis overview, clinical pipeline, commercial portfolio, and strategic vision Marketed RLTs Abb: CVRM: Cardiovascular, Renal and Metabolism; GEP NET: Gastroenteropancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors; mCRPC: Metastatic Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer; mHSPC: Metastatic Hormone-Sensitive Prostate Cancer; PSMA: Prostate Membrane Specific Antigen; SSTR: Somatostatin Receptor

Market Opportunity & Commercial Landscape Objective: Assess the market potential, commercialization pathway, reimbursement environment, and key barriers influencing radiopharmaceutical adoption

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Radiopharmaceutical Market Snapshot (2026-2035) Assessing market size, growth drivers, competitive advantage, and barrier in the global radiopharmaceutical sector MARKET SIZE ($B) 7.9 8.6 9.4 10.2 11.1 12.1 13.2 14.3 15.6 17.0 2026 2027 2028 2029 2030 2031 2032 2033 2034 2035 $17B 8.9% Asia-Pacific Projected market size by 2035 CAGR, 2026–2035 Fastest growing region KEY HIGHLIGHTS KEY INSIGHTS Growth Drivers Industry Landscape Oncology is the largest application, with North America leading and Asia-Pacific emerging as the fastest growing region on expanding nuclear medicine infrastructure Technetium-99m continues to dominate usage, while Gallium-68 is the fastest- growing isotope; recent M&A activity reflects strong investment in isotope production and theranostic capabilities Market Transition Key Barrier Competitive Advantage Views differ on the diagnostic vs therapeutic split, but theranostics is accelerating the shift toward targeted radiopharmaceutical therapies GE HealthCare's and AstraZeneca's recent acquisitions show isotope supply and manufacturing are now as strategic as drug discovery itself Isotope supply constraints and short radionuclide half-lives raise barriers to entry, favoring firms with established production networks

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com CHALLENGE SUPPORTING EVIDENCE STRATEGIC IMPLICATION Isotope Supply Concentration Only 8-10 of ~60 active global research reactors are the major producers of medical radionuclides A reactor going offline is a recurring risk, not a rare one, any pipeline asset depends on its isotope sourcing plan Infrastructure & Workforce Capacity Constraints An estimated 70-280 additional RPT treatment centers are needed for ~41,500 eligible NET/Prostate Cancer patients. Workforce shortages and unequal distribution limit access to RPT Market expansion is constrained by treatment-center capacity and specialist availability, not just regulatory approval or reimbursement Regulatory Pathway Complexity Dual regulatory pathways for drug and radiation safety complicate radiopharmaceutical review; US FDA review involves multiple divisions with NRC oversight Requires coordinated regulatory, manufacturing, and radiation- safety planning Alpha-Emitter Supply Risk Limited supply of alpha-emitting isotopes (eg: Pb-212 and Ac- 225) is driving companies such as Perspective Therapeutics and Actinium Pharmaceuticals to invest in proprietary production capabilities Decentralized isotope production is emerging as a competitive differentiator, particularly among smaller and mid-cap developers Adverse Event Underreporting Adverse event underreporting is driven by time constraints, low staff awareness and weak reporting culture; 43% of reported ADRs in a French database were serious, including 12 deaths Low reported ADR rates should be interpreted with caution due to potential underreporting Emerging Generic Competition PNT2003 (radioequivalent to LUTATHERA) received tentative US FDA approval, with final approval pending patent litigation First-generation RPTs may begin to face pricing and market-share pressures as generic competition emerges 1 3 4 5 6 2 Radiopharmaceuticals: What Could Hinder Market Growth Abb: ADR: Adverse Drug Reaction; NET: Neuroendocrine Tumor; NRC: Nuclear Regulatory Commission; RPT: Radiopharmaceutical Therapy

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Payer Dynamics Cost-Effectiveness Structural Hurdles Unique to Radioactive Drugs ❖ Diagnostic radiopharmaceuticals: Under Medicare OPPS, CMS separately reimburses qualifying diagnostic RPTs above the annual packaging threshold ($630 in CY2025; $655 in CY2026), while products below the threshold continue to receive packaged payment ▪ Diagnostic RPTS above the $655/day threshold are reimbursed using Mean Unit Cost (MUC), as CMS declined to adopt ASP-based payment for diagnostics in the CY2026 final rule ❖ Therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals: CMS reimburses payable therapeutic RPTs at ASP+6% with novel RPTs requiring appropriate HCPCS/ APC codes and clear payment methodology ❖ Budget impact models are mandatory in Spain and Italy, while cost-effectiveness models are strongly recommended to support pricing decisions. Although not mandatory, RWE can help demonstrate long-term outcomes and support sustainable pricing ❖ Eg: LUTATHERA was recommended by NICE under a confidential commercial arrangement, whereas PLUVICTO received a negative recommendation in its initial NICE appraisal, illustrating the importance of strong clinical and economic evidence in reimbursement decisions ❖ Cost-effectiveness models in the US focus on how RPTs reduce non-beneficial high-cost treatments and downstream toxicity, framing value in terms of budget impact and financial toxicity reduction rather than formal HTA pass/fail decisions ❖ Radiopharmaceuticals have no inventory buffer, unlike conventional drugs, their raw material and final product have only a few days of shelf life, forcing a 'just-in-time' supply chain, leaving providers unable to buffer against inadequate reimbursement the way other drug classes can ❖ An estimated 70-280 additional RPT treatment centers are needed for ~41,500 eligible patients, while specialized infrastructure (authorized user physicians, radiation safety oversight & dedicated facilities) continues to constrain delivery capacity Radiopharmaceuticals Market Access Payer economics, cost-effectiveness arguments and structural hurdles unique to radioactive drugs Abb: APC: Ambulatory Payment Classification; ; ASP: Average Sales Price; CMS: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services; CY: Calendar Year; HCPCS: Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System; HTA: Health Technology Assessment; NICE: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence; OPPS: Outpatient Prospective Payment System; RPT: Radiopharmaceutical Therapy High-cost diagnostic radiopharmaceuticals are paid separately using mean unit cost, while therapeutic agents are reimbursed at ASP+6% when appropriately coded Country-specific economic evidence, especially budget impact and cost-effectiveness determines reimbursement success more than clinical data alone Approval & reimbursement alone do not guarantee patient access, commercial scale depends on treatment-center capacity, specialized infrastructure, licensing and a trained workforce

Innovation & Clinical Development Objective: Evaluate emerging therapies, recent clinical evidence, and approved products to understand the evolving radiopharmaceutical pipeline

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Company Snapshot Clinical-stage radiopharmaceutical company advancing targeted alpha therapies using its proprietary Pb-212 platform, integrating theranostic imaging and treatment to improve patient selection and precision tumor targeting Results at a Glance: [212Pb]VMT01 Phase 1/2a (Melanoma) Early clinical responses in heavily pre-treated melanoma, combined with a favorable safety profile, provide initial clinical validation of Perspective’s Pb-212 targeted alpha therapy platform beyond its lead NET program Efficacy Endpoints Safety Endpoints Endpoint Result Evaluable Patients 22 Complete Response (CR) 0 Partial Response (PR) 1 (4.5%) Stable Disease (SD) 9 (40.9%) Progressive Disease (PD) 12 (54.5%) Disease Control Rate (CR + PR + SD) 45.5% (10/22) Progression-Free Survival 4 patients achieved PFS ≥6 months Antitumor Activity Observed primarily at the 3 mCi dose level Endpoint Result Dose-Limiting Toxicities (DLTs) None reported Serious Adverse Events (SAEs) All SAEs (including one Grade 5 SAE) were attributed to disease progression rather than treatment Grade 1 TEAEs 19.2% Grade 2 TEAEs 34.6% Grade 3 TEAEs 8/26 patients (30.8%): 5 on monotherapy and 3 on 3 mCi + nivolumab Overall Tolerability Generally safe and well tolerated Clinical Development: Radiopharma at ASCO 2026 Phase 1/2a targeted alpha therapy data in heavily pre-treated, MC1R-positive metastatic melanoma

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Company Snapshot Clinical-stage radiopharmaceutical company advancing targeted alpha therapies using its proprietary Pb-212 platform, integrating theranostic imaging and treatment to improve patient selection and precision tumor targeting Results at a Glance: [212Pb]VMT-α-NET Phase 1/2a (GEP-NETs), data cut-off Mar 4, 2026, Efficacy Population-25 patients (Cohort 1: n=2; Cohort 2: n=23) Deepening responses, a 72% progression-free-and-alive rate, and a favorable safety profile across dose escalation provide early clinical validation of Perspective's Pb-212 targeted alpha platform as its lead NET program advances toward a registration-enabling study Efficacy Endpoint Result Comments Objective Response Rate (ORR) 43% (10/23) Investigator-assessed RECIST v1.1 in first half of Cohort 2 Complete Responses (CR) 0 No complete responses reported Partial Responses (PR) 10 patients Includes one additional new confirmed responder since ASCO GI 2026 Disease Control High Most remaining patients achieved stable disease Tumor Shrinkage Continued deepening 9 patients experienced further tumor shrinkage since the ESMO 2025 analysis Progression-Free and Alive 18/25 patients (72%) Across efficacy-evaluable Cohorts 1 and 2 at latest follow-up Durability Responses continued to deepen over time Follow-up remains ongoing Safety Endpoint Result Patients Evaluated 64 Dose-Limiting Toxicities (DLTs) None observed Grade 5 Treatment-Related Adverse Events None Serious Renal Toxicity None reported Grade ≥3 Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events (TEAEs) 23 patients (36%) Overall Tolerability Generally, well tolerated across dose cohorts Clinical Development: Radiopharma at AACR 2026 Updated Phase 1/2a interim data across three dose cohorts in SSTR2-positive neuroendocrine tumors Abb: GEP NET: Gastroenteropancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors

For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Product: ITM-11 (Solucin/ n.c.a. 177Lu- edotreotide/ n.c.a. 177Lu-DOTATOC) Indication: Grade 1/2, SSTR+ GEP-NETs Mechanism of Action: PRRT-SSTR2 agonist labeled with n.c.a. ¹⁷⁷Lu Route of Administration: Intravenous infusion (IV) Dose / Regimen: 7.5 ± 0.7 GBq IV q3mo (≤4 cycles), with nephroprotective amino acids Regulatory Milestone Timeline Note: ITM-11 is investigational - not yet approved by any regulatory authority Key Insights ✓ COMPETE trial beat Everolimus, but ITM-11’s (a beta radioisotope) real competitor once approved is LUTATHERA - same isotope, same target, same indication, same infrastructure ✓ Unlike PLUVICTO (drug bought first, isotope supply chased after), ITM built the therapy on its own existing Lu-177 manufacturing base, a vertically integrated model ✓ If approved in Aug 2026, ITM-11 would be the first new RPT since PLUVICTO (2022); the open question is whether it expands the capacity-constrained PRRT infusion grid or redistributes existing Lu-177 volume Risk to watch ✓ ITM-11 showed a small survival edge (63.4 vs 58.7 months), but it wasn't statistically significant, patient crossover may be why. INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com O V E R V I E W Standard timelines are too slow for today's pipelines For targeted therapies serving small patient subsets, the traditional development path is simply unfeasible; designations exist to provide regulatory flexibility through adaptive trial designs, faster reviews and commercial incentives P A T H W A Y S US FDA vs EMA at a Glance US FDA is more flexible, accepting early-stage and real- world data; EMA requires larger, more rigorous studies. This divergence makes early designation planning critical for global drug developers T R E N D S Designation Trends ODD are currently the safest, most rewarding pathways; ODD offers near-certain retention with 7-year exclusivity while RMAT is growing fast with ~354% grant growth, reflecting rapid growth of innovative therapies like CGT B U S I N E S S I M P A C T Strategic Value of Stacking Combining ODD + BTD + Priority Review can compress time-to-market by 2-4 years, add $100M+ in lifecycle value, and boost M&A premiums by 20-40%, making designations a core business strategy, not just a regulatory step R E F O R M S 2026 Reforms Reshaping the Field The Catalyst orphan exclusivity reversal opens previously blocked rare disease markets to competition; PRV program is extended to 2029; EMA PRIME now has mandatory pre-submission checkpoints and psychedelic therapies are fast-tracked via executive order with $50M in federal funding Executive Summary INSIGHTS CORNER

Regulatory Landscape & Pathway Architecture (US FDA & EMA Designation Framework) INSIGHTS CORNER

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com The Strategic Importance of US FDA and EMA Designations in 2026 Overview • Designations are special statuses granted to drug candidates by regulatory authorities, such as the US FDA in the United States and the CHMP/EMA in Europe, based on their intended indications and development needs • These designations are typically awarded to therapies targeting serious or life-threatening conditions, addressing unmet medical needs, and are intended to facilitate and expedite the drug development, review and approval processes Navigating Regulatory Divergence The US FDA is increasingly flexible, often accepting real-world evidence and single-arm trials for accelerated pathways. The EMA, however, generally demands larger, more comprehensive datasets with active comparators and longer follow-up periods. Designations force early alignment with these differing expectations Complex Targeted Therapies For highly targeted oncology pipelines such as next-generation inhibitors for EGFR-mutant advanced Lung cancer the standard 10 to 15-year development lifecycle is too slow. These therapies target specific patient subsets, meaning traditional large-scale trials are often unfeasible. Designations provide the regulatory flexibility needed to utilize adaptive trial designs and novel biomarkers Harmonizing Cross-Border Strategy Because the EMA requires consensus across member states, early engagement through PRIME helps sponsors structure their clinical plans. This ensures that data collected from investigators and KOLs across key European markets, such as Italy or Croatia, will hold up under centralized EMA scrutiny

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com US FDA Designations: An Overview Fast Track Designation Breakthrough Therapy Designation Priority Review Designation Orphan Drug Designation Accelerated Approval Review Program Overview When to Apply US FDA Response Timeline Features Additional Considerations It is a process intended to facilitate the development & expedites regulatory review of drugs, to treat serious conditions that address unmet medical need With IND, or after; no later than pre-BLA or pre-NDA meeting Within 60 calendar days of FTD request receipt Frequent meeting with US FDA, eligibility for accelerated approval & priority review, rolling review Designation may be withdrawn if product no longer satisfies fast track qualifying criteria Designation With IND or after; no later than the end of P2 meeting It is a process designed to accelerate the development & regulatory review of drugs based on clinically significant endpoint Designation Within 60 calendar days of BTD request receipt All FTD features, intensive guidance on an efficient drug development program, organizational commitment; rolling review Designation may be removed if product no longer satisfies BTD qualifying criteria With original BLA, NDA, or efficacy supplement Designation Within 60 calendar days of receipt of original BLA, NDA, or efficacy supplement Shortens US FDA application review timeline to 6 months compared to 10 months for a standard review Designation will be granted upon filing of original BLA, NDA, or efficacy supplement Within 90 days of ODD request receipt At any time in its drug development process, prior to submission of marketing application It is granted to drugs, (including biologics) intended for the prevention, diagnosis, or treatment of diseases affecting fewer than 200,000 individuals (rare disease) in US Designation 25% tax credits for qualified clinical trials, waiver of NDA/BLA user fees, eligibility for 7-year marketing exclusivity US FDA perform a distinct disease assessment based on MOA, pathophysiology, etiology, treatment options & prognosis At an early stage of clinical development It is a pathway allowed faster approval of drugs to treat serious conditions that fill an unmet medical need Approval pathway - Include drugs has an effect on a surrogate or an intermediate clinical endpoint that is reasonably likely to predict a drug’s clinical benefit Requires submission of promotional materials, post- marketing confirmatory trials, expedited withdrawal if eligibility criteria not met An original application or efficacy supplement for a drug treating serious condition. If approved, would provide significant improvement in safety or effectiveness Abbreviations: BTD: Breakthrough Therapy Designation; FTD: Fast Track Designation; ODD: Orphan Drug Designation

For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com EMA Designations: An Overview Orphan Drug Designation Accelerated Assessment Conditional Marketing Authorisation PRIME (priority medicines) Exceptional Circumstances Overview Eligibility Criteria Timeline/ Review Impact Additional Considerations Orphan drug designation granted to substances intended for the treatment, prevention, or diagnosis of rare and serious conditions Accelerated assessment reduces the review time for marketing- authorization application required by EMA CHMP EMA grants conditional marketing authorization to medicine that addresses an unmet medical need of patients based on less comprehensive data than normally required PRIME is an EMA initiative, facilitates the development of medicines targeting unmet medical needs by demonstrating meaningful improvement in clinical outcomes A type of marketing authorization granted to medicines when full efficacy and safety data cannot be generated under normal conditions of use US FDA responds within 30 days of request receipt CHMP can reduce marketing authorization timeframe from 210 days to 150 days Authorization valid for one year and can be renewed annually CHMP responds within 40 days from start of the procedure Authorization valid for five year and can be reassessed annually If a drug treat, prevent, or diagnose a life-threatening disease; disease must not affect >5 in 10,000 people in EU; no satisfactory method of diagnosis, prevention or treatment exists, if method exists drug have significant benefit over existing therapies If product is of major interest for public health and therapeutic innovation Positive benefit-risk balance, applicant will be able to provide comprehensive data post-authorization, fulfils an unmet medical need If drug not yet authorized in EU; no treatment option exists, or if a drug can offer major therapeutic advantage over existing treatments with request submitted to EMA during exploratory phase of clinical trial For extremely rare indications, if comprehensive data cannot provide, data collection not possible or unethical Scientific advice (eg: research protocol, technical assistance), market exclusivity for 10- years, fee reductions; Eligible for standard marketing authorization after submission of complete clinical data - Required submission of further clinical dataset in future Potential for accelerated assessment, early appointment of rapporteur, meetings with rapporteur & experts to discuss development plan Typically, not lead to full dossier completion & therefore not become standard marketing authorization Designation Review Program Approval pathway Designation Approval pathwayNature of Program

Competitive moat (ODD + BTD + PR) The 25% tax credit on clinical trial costs and 7-year exclusivity can be worth $100M+ over a product's lifecycle Financial strategy (ODD) ODD exclusivity prevents US FDA from approving a competitor's same drug for the same indication for 7 years BTD combined with PR can get to market 2-4 years before a competitor on the standard pathway, locking in prescriber habits and payer formularies before the competition even files Investor and M&A (BTD) Operational (FTD + BTD) FTD rolling review means US FDA has already reviewed 40- 60% of the NDA before the formal filing date, compressing the real review timeline far beyond what the 6-month PR clock suggests BTD makes US FDA a co-developer: cross-disciplinary team assignments, senior reviewer access, and collaborative trial design that dramatically reduces the risk of a Complete Response Letter at submission BTD alone raises acquisition premiums by roughly 20-40%. Stacked designations function as a regulatory "seal of quality" that de-risks assets for large pharma acquirers BTD + ODD programs consistently command 2 to 3× higher IPO valuations than no- designation programs in the same indication Stacking ODD, FTD, BTD and Priority Review transforms a program into a strategic asset that accelerates time to market, amplifies exclusivity and tax benefits, and boosts investor and M&A value while de-risking FDA review

However, it also highlights the regulatory risk of accelerated approvals, indications can be withdrawn if confirmatory trials fail to verify clinical benefit, as occurred in Urothelial cancer Pre-2020 Apr 2020 Apr 2021 Feb 2023 Oct 2024 Fast Track Designation: TNBC; NSCLC; mUC; SCLC Breakthrough Therapy Designation: mTNBC FTD and BTD helped speed up development with more frequent US FDA interactions and faster alignment Approved Indications: ≥2L mTNBC and Pre-Treated HR+/HER2- mBC Pipeline: 1L TNBC (Filed), 1L NSCLC (P3), SCLC (P3), 2L mEC (P3) mTNBC after ≥2 prior therapies Accelerated approval based on ORR and DoR in P2 study First US FDA-approved anti-Trop-2 ADC. The US FDA approved this application 6 weeks ahead Pre-Treated HR+/HER2- mBC Regular approval under Project Orbis, FDA collaborated with Australian TGA, Health Canada and Switzerland’s Swissmedic (PR for sBLA accepted on Oct 2022) Approval in less than 6 months. item.title: Octavus Insights Corner - Gene Therapy (May 2026)
item.description: Octavus Insights Corner for May 2026: gene therapy.
item.content:encoded:
Month: May 2026 Presenter: Team Octavus THERAPY 2025-26 HIGHLIGHTSGENE Insights Corner CGT Within

AGENDA Content This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com INSIGHTS CORNER Scientific Foundations of Gene Therapy 05 Market Pulse of Gene Therapy Gene Therapy: Landscape & Upcoming Milestones 10 15 Regulatory & Approval Landscape 20 Tracking Spark Therapeutics Growth Within Gene Therapy Ecosystem 23 Challenges, Risks & Strategic Assessment 25 Future Frontier of Gene Therapy 28 Glossary of Abbreviations 30

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.comThis presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Highlights from AACR-25 (May, 25) US Tariff impact on Pharma industries (Jun, 25) EULAR-25: Key insights of Psoriatic Arthritis (Jul, 25) Antibody Drug Conjugate: The next big investment in Oncology (Aug, 25) Animal Health (Oct, 25) Obesity deep dive (Nov ,25) GLP-1 and GIP (Dec, 25) Hematological Highlights from ASH 2025 (Jan, 26) China Biotech’s Global Positioning from JPM-26 (Feb,26) BIOSIMILARS RISING: The Catalyst For A New Age In Biologics Therapies (Mar,26) Cell Therapy Within CGT (Apr, 26) Additional: 1 Beautiful Bill PRIOR ISSUES INSIGHTS CORNER

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com INSIGHTS CORNER Executive Summary Part 2 of the CGT landscape, with primary focus on gene therapy From experiment to platform: Gene therapy has shifted from high-risk experimentation to a strategic platform across rare diseases, hemoglobinopathies, ophthalmology, neuromuscular and emerging CNS indications Diverging technology archetypes and Vectors as core infrastructure: The landscape is fragmenting across in vivo vs ex vivo, AAV vs non-viral/LVV, and gene-editing modalities (CRISPR, base editing), creating distinct competitive archetypes and vectors sit at the center of the biotech stack with AAV being the workhorse for durable in vivo delivery Capital and deal momentum: The funding and deal environment is maturing, with ~$24B in disclosed funding across 154 rounds and ~$25B in 2025 deal value, skewed toward late-stage and approved assets in oncology and rare disease platforms Execution as the bottleneck: Vector supply, CMC comparability, immunogenicity, redosing constraints and manufacturing scale-up are now as decisive as the headline clinical data in determining long-term winners Clinical and regulatory tailwinds: Gene therapy trials are rising steadily (over 160 new trials annually by 2025) in major markets, while FDA, EMA and ICH roll out flexible CMC, rare-population trial and long-term follow-up frameworks that de-risk development

Scientific Foundations of Gene Therapy (Core concepts, technologies & therapeutic strategies) INSIGHTS CORNER 5

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Gene Therapy: Key Approaches Gene Addition/ Gene Augmentation Gene Editing Gene Silencing/ Gene Inactivation Gene Replacement/ Gene Correction Gene addition is a widely explored gene therapy approach for treating monogenic disorders caused by mutations in one or both copies of a gene. The strategy involves delivering functional or healthy copies of the gene into a patient’s cells using a vector. E.g. Hemophilia B is treated by delivering a functional copy of the clotting factor IX (FIX) gene into liver cells using viral vectors, with the goal of restoring normal blood clotting activity. Gene silencing or gene knockdown, is an approach used to reduce or inhibit the expression of specific disease-causing genes at the transcriptional or translational level. E.g. In Huntington’s disease, RNAi can target the mutant huntingtin gene by degrading its mRNA, thereby lowering the production of the toxic huntingtin protein. Gene editing is a technique of creating specific breaks in the DNA using specialized techniques, with or without repair signals. Two main approaches to gene editing are gene disruption/inactivation (gene is switched off) & gene correction/insertion (gene is repaired or a new genetic sequence is added). E.g. CRISPR-Cas9 has become most widely adopted gene-editing technology due to its high precision & efficiency. Gene replacement is a therapeutic approach that restores normal cell function by replacing a defective gene with a functional copy. This strategy is particularly useful for treating genetic disorders caused by mutations that result in the absence or malfunction of specific proteins. E.g. Treatment of severe SCID, commonly referred to as “bubble boy disease”. Antisense technology & RNA interference (RNAi) are most widely used strategies for achieving gene knockdown. Decoding the scientific approaches behind advanced genetic therapies Gene therapy is an advanced therapeutic approach to deliver exogenous genes that compensate for or replace the function of defective genes., offering a potential treatment strategy beyond conventional therapies such as pharmaceuticals, radiotherapy or surgery

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Somatic Gene Therapy Germline Gene Therapy Somatic gene therapy corrects genetic disorders via targeted modification of non-germline somatic cells. The approach typically involves ex vivo isolation of dysfunctional cells, followed by their transduction or transfection with a functional wild-type gene copy. These genetically corrected cells are then reinfused into the patient, where they engraft and restore the deficient gene product's function Germline gene therapy targets reproductive cells (sperm, eggs, or early embryos) to permanently alter heritable genetic makeup, aiming to prevent disease or introduce enhancing alleles. Unlike somatic approaches, it remains highly controversial, with no human trials conducted due to an informal moratorium in the scientific community Key Features Key Features ▪ Non-heritable: Changes stay within the treated patient only ▪ Minimal ethics: Genetically straightforward, widely accepted ▪ Clinically proven multiple US FDA/EMA: Approved treatments exist ▪ Heritable: Changes pass to all offspring & descendants ▪ Unpredictable: Long-lasting, irreversible, species-wide effects ▪ Global ban: Not in experimental stage; ethically prohibited Approved Molecules Approved Molecules KRELSADI, ITVISAM, WASKYRA, ZOLGENSMA, LUXTURNA, KYMRIAH, YESCARTA, HEMGENIX, SKYSONA are some of the approved therapies No jurisdiction has approved germline genome editing due to safety & ethical concerns. Modifications to germline cells become heritable, potentially perpetuating adverse effects across generations. Hence, most EU nations have ratified the Oviedo Convention, banning heritable human genetic modification Types of Gene Therapy INSIGHTS CORNER

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com Dimension Ex vivo In vivo Targeting precision High-defined cell population Variable-off-target tissues a concern Immune evasion Favourable, avoids allogenic rejection Challenging; pre-existing AAV antibodies limits eligibility Manufacturing Patient-specific, vein-to- vein 30-90 days Off-the-shelf vector production; weeks to manufacture at scale Cost of Goods Very high Moderate Scalability Low High Approved products CAR-T (KYMRIAH, YESCARTA), gene- modified HSCs (ZYNTEGLO, CASGEVY) AAV (LUXTURNA, ZOLGENSMA, ROCTAVIAN, HEMGENIX); LNP- mRNA (CASGEVY-adjacent) Therapeutic areas Oncology (haem), monogenic blood disorders, autoimmune (emerging) Ophthalmology, neurology, hepatology, rare metabolic; expanding to CNS, muscle Market access Restricted, needs specialized treatment centers and cold-chain logistics Broader, simpler logistics, outpatient potential for some indications Redosability Autologous re- manufacturing costly Limited; anti-capsid antibodies typically prevent redosing with same serotype Why Shift is happening: Scientific Advances: Better delivery systems with advances in viral vectors (AAV, lentivirus) and non-viral delivery (LNPs, nanoparticles). CRISPR & base-editing tools optimized for in vivo use. Economic Pressure: Reduced manufacturing complexity & cost, with greater scalability to treat larger patient populations. Patient Needs: In vivo approaches offer the potential for faster treatment, reduced procedural invasiveness & broader access for patients. Strategic Implications: • In vivo gene therapy is poised to rapidly capture monogenic disease indications e.g., Hemophilia, Metabolic disorders & Ophthalmic conditions given the established clinical track record of AAV-based delivery in these settings • However, Ex vivo autologous approaches will remain the dominant modality in hematologic oncology in the near term, as CAR-T efficacy data are too strong to displace without equivalent in vivo data MODALITY COMPARISON Ex Vivo to In Vivo: Redefining the Future

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com From Viruses to Nanocarriers Parameters Viral Non-viral Immunogenicity Highly immunogenic Less immunogenic Tissue transduction Easily transduce different cells & tissues Poor transduction potentials Genetic modification Requires genetic mutations May not require genetic alteration Chemical modification Tentative Required Cell type Somatic & germline Mostly somatic Examples Retroviral, lentiviral & adeno-associated viral vectors, etc. LNPs, Plasmid, virosomes, etc. Viral Vector Non-viral Vector Viral vs Non-viral Vectors Comparison of viral and non-viral vectors Non-viral vectors offer advantages such as low toxicity, reduced mutagenesis risk, cost-effective, scalable production and low immunogenicity, providing key safety benefits over viral approaches. However, they often exhibit lower transfection efficiency, limited target specificity & delayed gene expression timelines. Most widely researched non-viral delivery methods include chemical disruption, electroporation & polymer-based vectors. Vectors serve as a delivery backbone of CGT, enables transfer of genetic material to modify or correct defective genes for the treatment of genetic disorders, cancers & other diseases. In the 21st century, advances in viral vector manufacturing have significantly improved the safety & efficiency of these therapies. Today, both viral & non- viral vectors continue to drive innovation & expand the therapeutic potential of gene therapy Viral vectors offer highly efficient & targeted gene delivery, enable long-lasting gene expression and are generally non- replicating & minimally destructive to cells. However, their limited loading capacity restricts the delivery of larger genes & may induce immunogenic responses. At present, viral vectors are the most commonly used delivery vehicles in US FDA approved therapies.

It provides recommendations to help developers collect sufficient clinical safety & efficacy data. Also, ensures that the therapy is manufactured with proper quality standards & is suitable for its intended use ❑ Jan, 2026: From Lab to Market Faster: Flexible CMC Framework for CGT: US FDA is using a more flexible approach to CMC requirements for CGT, like clinical development, commercial specifications & process validation flexibilities, to help companies better prepare for BLA submission & approval ❑ Sep, 2025: Fast-Track Regulatory Programs for Regenerative Medicine: This guidance helps developers of regenerative medicine therapies for serious or life-threatening conditions understand the US FDA expedited programs, including RMAT designation. It explains how to use accelerated approval pathways, provides advice on clinical development & highlights opportunities to engage with CBER to speed up the development & review process ❑ Sep, 2025: Beyond Approval: Capturing Real-World Data for CGT Products: The aim is to explain methods for collecting safety and efficacy data for CGT products after approval, including LFTU (e.g., 15 years). (This guidance does not cover data collected to support the expansion of clinical indications) ❑ Sep, 2025: Innovative Trial Designs for CGT in Small & Rare Populations: US FDA provide recommendations to sponsors planning clinical trials for CGT products used in small or rare patient populations. It explains FDA requirements and outlines different trial designs (Adaptive/Bayesian trial design & Master protocols) and surrogate endpoints that can be used to generate the clinical evidence needed for product approval. (This document elaborates on the US FDA previously established guidance principles) ❑ Dec, 2025: Future Guideline Roadmap for ATMPs: ICH CGTDG, first established key guiding principles for ATMPs & then created a roadmap for CGT, focusing on priority areas that need better harmonization along with recommendations for new or updated guidelines ❑ May, 2025: ATMP Comparability: Proposed New ICH Q5E Annex: ICH Multidisciplinary guideline (ICH Q5E) is proposed to address the unique development & regulatory challenges of ATMPs, including CGTs, with a focus on ensuring comparability when their manufacturing processes changes ❑ Jan, 2025: EMA Sets Standards for ATMP Clinical Trials (Effective July 1, 2025): EMA has introduced a multidisciplinary guideline outlining the development, manufacturing, quality control, non-clinical & clinical requirements for investigational ATMPs. It explains what data and structure are needed for a CTA (both early and late- stage studies) helping companies prepare for a MAA ❑ Mar, 2025: EMA Revises GMP Framework for ATMPs: EMA has released a concept paper proposing updates to Part IV of the EU GMP guidelines for ATMPs, aiming to align with current Annex 1, while maintaining flexibility in ATMP production How updates from US FDA, EMA & ICH are redefining cell & gene therapy?

Challenges, Risks & Strategic Assessment (Limitations, barriers, opportunities & future readiness) INSIGHTS CORNER 25

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com 1. Safe and precise delivery to the right tissue - Efficient, tissue-specific delivery of DNA/RNA or gene-editing machinery remains one of the biggest barriers, especially for organs like the brain and heart. Systemically administered vectors must survive degradation, cross biological barriers (e.g., blood–brain barrier), and avoid off-target transduction, which current AAV and nanoparticle systems still do imperfectly 2. Immunogenicity and limited re-dosing - Viral vectors such as AAV can trigger innate and adaptive immune responses against capsid and/or transgene, which may cause toxicity and can block repeat dosing. Pre-existing neutralizing antibodies and treatment-induced immunity often exclude patients from trials or prevent them from receiving a second dose if the first one is sub-therapeutic 3. Off-target effects and long-term safety - CRISPR and related editors can introduce unintended genomic changes, raising concerns about genotoxicity, oncogenesis, and other adverse effects that may only emerge years later. Reviews emphasize that, despite improved guide design and high-fidelity nucleases, fully characterizing off-target edits in vivo and predicting their long-term consequences remains an unresolved challenge 4. Manufacturing scalability, cost, and quality control - Current manufacturing processes for viral vectors and complex delivery systems are expensive, capacity-limited, and technically demanding, which constrains patient access and slows development. 2025-2026 analyses highlight persistent pain points around large-scale GMP production, assay comparability, and CMC expectations, all of which add significant cost and time to each program 5. Clinical, regulatory, and access complexity - Gene therapy programs often face difficult trial design and endpoint selection, especially in rare diseases, alongside extensive long-term safety follow-up requirements. Even after approval, adoption can remain limited due to complex regulatory expectations, specialized treatment-center requirements, high costs, and reimbursement uncertainty INSIGHTS CORNER Gene Therapy’s Biggest Hurdles

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com S W O T • High cost: Gene therapies carry high upfront prices to recover R&D from one-time dosing (e.g. GLYBERA ~€1M), leading to reimbursement barriers and market withdrawal • Immune response challenge: Viral vector gene therapies (e.g. AAV) trigger CD8+ T-cell responses and inflammation, often requiring steroid-based immunosuppression across hepatic, systemic and ocular indications • Long-term durability uncertainty & limited RWE: Gene therapies face LTFU challenges, with limited real-world data to assess long-term efficacy and late safety risks (e.g. oncogenesis) • Convenience: Potentially curative, one-time treatments for monogenic and select acquired diseases, reducing long-term disease burden • Rare disease success: Demonstrated efficacy of AAV-based gene replacement in rare disorders, e.g. ZOLGENSMA, a one-time SMN1-targeted therapy for infants with SMA • Expanding disease reach: Gene therapy is moving beyond rare monogenic disease into oncology, monogenic disorders (e.g. SMA), polygenic conditions (e.g. Autism), neurodegenerative diseases (e.g. Parkinson’s) & infectious diseases like HIV • Market size: Growing R&D and investment pipeline, with accelerating global approvals projecting double-digit market CAGR through the next decade • Rare genetic diseases: ~95% of rare genetic diseases lack approved treatments, representing significant unmet need addressable through gene therapy targeting root genetic defects • Advancing non-viral delivery (LNPs): Lipid nanoparticles enable safer, scalable and less immunogenic mRNA/siRNA delivery, supporting approved therapies and enabling repeat dosing and broader in vivo applications • Reimbursement failures: Payment-model failures can derail gene therapies despite regulatory approval (e.g. GLYBERA withdrawn in EU due to lack of demand, not safety) • Regulatory bodies demanding real-world outcomes data: Increasing demand for robust real-world and long-term outcomes data delays approvals, constrains reimbursement & adds pricing uncertainty for gene therapies • Competition: Competitive pressure from other advanced modalities (e.g. RNA therapies, small molecule or biologic functional cures) STRENGTHS WEAKNESSES OPPORTUNITIES THREATS Gene Therapy: SWOT Analysis

Future Frontier of Gene Therapy (Long term outlook, innovation trends and future potential) INSIGHTS CORNER 28

INSIGHTS CORNER This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com 1. Shift toward in vivo gene editing Gene therapy is moving from ex vivo edited cells toward in vivo delivery of genome editors directly to target tissues, aiming for simpler, one-time treatments. A 2025 review highlights rapid translation of CRISPR, base, and prime editors into in vivo applications across genetic diseases, beyond earlier ex vivo only approaches. 2. Precision targeting & safer editing platforms Precision targeting and safer editing platforms - The field is moving toward next- generation editors and delivery systems that can selectively reach target tissues, reduce off-target effects, and avoid the risks associated with less controlled genome modification. Base editing, prime editing, and engineered delivery vehicles are expected to play a central role in making gene therapy safer and more precise. 3. Non-viral delivery Next-generation non-viral carriers (lipid nanoparticles, exosomes/extracellular vesicles, virus-like particles, and protein-based carriers) are emerging to reduce immunogenicity and enable repeat dosing. A 2026 open-access review describes a coming "age of CRISPR delivery with non-viral biologics," emphasizing engineered exosomes and other biologic nanoparticles as key to safer, more flexible in vivo editing. 4. Integration of AI & data-driven development AI and machine learning are increasingly used to design vectors and guides, predict off-target risk, optimize dose, and streamline clinical-trial operations, and are expected to be deeply embedded in future gene-therapy R&D. 2026 life-sciences forecasts describe advanced AI as the "engine" of next-gen cell and gene therapy, impacting discovery, trial design, and real-world evidence generation for regulatory and access decisions. 5. Broader indications, access, & equity focus Gene therapy is projected to move from rare monogenic diseases into more common indications (neuromuscular, autoimmune, cardiovascular, and metabolic diseases) while simultaneously tackling access barriers. Policy and market-access trend reports from 2024–2026 highlight outcome-based payment models, community-site delivery, and global trial diversification as crucial to making these high-value therapies more widely available. This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com INSIGHTS CORNER Why Cell Therapy is Trending? Curative and regenerative potential (beyond oncology) 1 2 3 4 5 Rapid growth in oncology, with a shift toward solid tumors • Global oncology incidence is rising steeply, and many patients still relapse or become resistant to current drugs, creating strong demand for new modalities like CAR-T and other cell therapies • Since 2020, the number of CAR-T trials in solid tumors has increased substantially, reflecting growing sponsor efforts to translate CAR-T success beyond hematologic malignancies, despite the higher biological and clinical risks associated with solid tumor targets and microenvironments Explosive increase in clinical trial activity overall • Since around 2017, the number of registered global industry-sponsored cell therapy trials has surged, with ~5,000 trials now listed across clinical trial database, and this activity is expected to continue rising over the next decade as innovation and investment expand across a broad range of therapeutic areas and indications • This volume signals that cell therapy is no longer a niche field; it is becoming a mainstream R&D pillar for big pharma, biotech's, and academic centers across many disease areas Manufacturing and scalability are unlocking the next growth wave • As trials and approvals grow, the focus is shifting from “can cell therapy work” to “how do we industrialize it?”, accelerating investment in scalable, reliable and more affordable manufacturing solutions • Advances in automation, allogeneic platforms and specialized CDMOs are rapidly transforming today's high-cost, manual and fragile process into standardized manufacturing platforms that can support broad patient access and global expansion of cell therapies Big-pharma partnerships are validating cell therapy • Big pharma and strategic partnerships are increasingly confirming the cell therapy space as a long-term, investable modality. Large pharmaceutical companies are entering multi-billion-dollar licensing deals, co-development agreements, and M&A transactions with specialized cell and gene therapy companies. These collaborations bring industrial-scale manufacturing, global commercial infrastructure, and late-stage clinical development ability that smaller players often lack. The steady flow of alliances and acquisitions signals that cell therapy is no longer viewed as an experimental niche but as a core pillar of future oncology and regenerative medicine portfolios • Cell therapies can potentially treat diseases with no known cure by repairing or replacing damaged tissue, including conditions like Vision loss, age-related Macular Degeneration and multiple sclerosis (MS) • Unlike treatments that only slow progression, early clinical data in MS, eye diseases, and Parkinson’s suggest that stem cell derived therapies may restore function, driving increased interest in these areas

Key Drivers Asia-Pacific Expansion - Expansion of research and development in biopharma, rising investments in advanced cell and gene therapy framework, rapid growth in clinical trial are driving Asia Pacific as a high-growth region. Clinical Pipeline - The cell and gene therapy is at a turning point, 900 CAR-T clinical trials started since 2020. From January to March 2025 there are 57% of the 79 new gene, cell, and RNA therapy trials were in oncology. Rising Occurrence of Chronic & Rare Diseases - The increasing prevalence of age-related diseases, chronic conditions, cancer, autoimmune disorders, and neurological disorders has intensified demand for effective cell-based treatments. Expanding Regulatory Approvals & Accelerated Pathways - Nearly 35% of regulatory approvals are linked to accelerated pathways, strengthening the market's growth trajectory. Regulatory acceleration programs are a significant factor influencing regional growth across the globe. Limitations of Traditional Treatments - Cell therapies provide an alternative to traditional organ transplants, which face severe limitations like donor shortages and rejection risks. This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com INSIGHTS CORNER CAR T-cell therapy is an immunotherapy in which T cells are genetically modified to recognize and destroy cancer cells, mainly for certain blood cancers. It includes: Autologous CAR-T: which uses the patient’s own engineered T cells with lower rejection risk Allogeneic CAR-T: which uses donor-derived “off-the- shelf” T cells that enable faster treatment but may carry risks of immune rejection or graft-versus-host reactions. CAR-T CELL THERAPY CAR-NK therapy is a cancer immunotherapy where natural killer (NK) cells are genetically engineered with CARs to target tumor antigens, enhancing cancer cell killing. These cells can come from donors, cord blood, or stem cells, enabling off-the-shelf treatment with lower risks of cytokine release syndrome and graft-versus-host disease than CAR-T therapy. CAR-NK CELL THERAPY Tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy is an adoptive cell immunotherapy where T cells isolated from a patient’s tumor are expanded in the laboratory and reinfused, often after lymphodepleting chemotherapy and with IL-2 support, to attack cancer cells. TIL THERAPY mRNA-based cell therapy delivers mRNA into cells to produce therapeutic proteins, enabling temporary expression without altering DNA and offering a safer alternative to viral gene delivery in therapies like CAR-T. mRNA-BASED CELL THERAPY TCR-T cell therapy is a cancer immunotherapy in which T cells are genetically engineered with high- affinity T-cell receptors (TCRs) to recognize tumor antigens presented by MHC molecules, enabling targeted immune destruction of cancer cells. TCR-T CELL THERAPY In vivo CAR-T generation delivers CAR-encoding genetic material directly into a patient’s T cells inside the body, programming them to become CAR-T cells and eliminating the need for ex vivo cell collection and engineering. IN VIVO CAR-T GENERATION TYPES OF EMERGING CELL THERAPY TECHNOLOGIES INSIGHTS CORNE

This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com INSIGHTS CORNER Evolution of CAR-T: From 1st, 2nd to Next Generation Summary • Earliest CAR design: scFv + CD3ζ (or FcγR) signaling domain • First proof that T cells can be redirected to tumor antigens • Addition of one co-stimulatory domain (CD28 or 4-1BB) + CD3ζ • Foundation of currently approved CAR-T therapies • Incorporate two co-stimulatory domains (e.g., CD28 + 4-1BB or OX40) • Armored CAR-T cells, that secrete cytokines upon activation • Add a third signal (cytokine signaling) • Advanced CARs with built-in cytokine receptor signaling (JAK- STAT pathway) • Designed to mimic natural T cell activation fully Working Mechanism • Recognize tumor antigen via scFv • Activate T cells through CD3ζ signaling only • No co-stimulation, incomplete activation • Provide two signals: • Antigen recognition (CD3ζ) • Co-stimulation (CD28 or 4-1BB) • Improves activation, proliferation, and survival • Combine signaling pathways to: • Enhance activation • Improve persistence • Reduce exhaustion • Recognize tumor, activate and release cytokines (e.g. IL-2, IL-12, etc) • Cytokines: • Enhance CAR-T function • Remodel tumor microenvironment • Recruit other immune cells • Provide three integrated signals: • CD3ζ → activation • Co-stimulation (e.g., CD28) • Cytokine signaling (via JAK- STAT pathway) • No need for external cytokines Impact • First to redirect T cell specificity to tumor antigens, proving concept in preclinical trials • Stronger T cell activation • Better persistence and expansion • Major clinical success (e.g., CD19- targeted therapies) • Approved therapies for leukemia and lymphoma (ABECMA, BREYANZI, etc) • Potentially stronger and more durable responses • Better expansion and persistence in some studies • Synergistic signaling effects • Clinical studies is ongoing for lymphoma (HD-CAR-1, WZTL-002, etc) • Overcome immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment • Improved activity in solid tumors • Promote antigen spreading and broader immunity • Enhanced persistence and proliferation • Continuous, controlled cytokine signaling • Reduced T cell exhaustion • Better persistence and expansion • Improved tumor infiltration (especially solid tumors) • More physiological Challenges • No co-stimulatory signal • Poor in vivo persistence • Weak and short-lived antitumor response • Limited clinical success • Risk of toxicity • No approved CAR-T • Toxicities: CRS (Cytokine release syndrome), Immune effector cell- associated neurotoxicity syndrome • Limited efficacy in solid tumor • Still risk of relapse (antigen loss) • Limited clinical evidence of superiority over 2G • No consistent improvement in durability • Tumor escape still possible (lack of antigen spreading) • High cost and complexity • High risk of systemic toxicity (CRS, off-tumor effects) • Difficult control of cytokine release • Preclinical success not fully predictive of human safety • Complex engineering • Still in early/preclinical stages • Safety concerns (CRS, cytokine overactivation) • Need for optimized dosing and regulation • Limited clinical validation 1st Generation 2nd Generation 3rd Generation 4th Generation 5th Generation

For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com INSIGHTS CORNER TIL Therapy Introduced Adoptive transfer of tumor- infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) is used to treat metastatic melanoma, demonstrating early success of T-cell based immunotherapy 1st Generation CAR-T Cells The first chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells are developed, enabling engineered T cells to recognize tumor antigens 2nd Generation CAR-T (CD28) Addition of the CD28 co- stimulatory domain improves T-cell activation, proliferation, and antitumor activity 2nd Generation CAR-T (4-1BB) Incorporation of the 4-1BB co- stimulatory domain enhances persistence and memory formation of CAR-T cells TCR-T Therapy Development T-cell receptor engineered therapies show potential in treating cancers such as metastatic melanoma 1st CD19 CAR-T Patient Clinical trials showed successful leukemia treatment with CD19- targeted CAR-T cells, leading to the development of 3rd generation CAR-T therapies 4th Generation CAR-T “Armored” CAR-T cells are engineered to secrete cytokines to enhance immune responses 1st CAR-T Approvals The FDA approves the first CAR-T therapy for lymphoma patients Expansion to Autoimmune Diseases CAR-T therapy begins to be explored for autoimmune disorders such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) Next-Generation Engineering Advanced CAR-T modifications are being developed to improve effectiveness, particularly against solid tumors Major cell therapy milestones The US FDA approved Lifileucel, the 1st TIL therapy for unresectable or metastatic melanoma, and Afamitresgene autoleucel, the 1st TCR-T therapy for a solid tumor (synovial sarcoma). Later, Obecabtagene autoleucel became the 7th approved CAR- T therapy for R/R B-cell ALL, while new CAR-T trials in AML targeting CD33, CD123, and CLL1 reported encouraging remission outcomes In vivo CAR-T cell engineering In vivo CAR-T engineering enables direct generation of CAR-T cells within patients, eliminating complex ex vivo manufacturing while maintaining strong and sustained antitumor activity. Early ASCO 2025, P1 data show promising signals in solid tumors, including B7H3-CAR-T in glioblastoma and GCC19CART in metastatic colorectal cancer (80% ORR at higher doses) 1988 1993 1998 2004 2006 2010 2012 2017 2021 2023 2024 2025 Cell Therapy Timeline INSIGHTS CORNE

For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com INSIGHTS CORNER Key Barriers Slowing Cell Therapy Trials 1 3 2 4 Safety, Manufacturing, and Regulatory Constraints Cell therapies often fail because the patient’s body environment can suppress or block therapeutic cells, reducing their ability to expand and function in vivo. Host-related factors such as immune regulation, prior treatments, and variable patient biology also contribute to reduced efficacy or relapse Limited In Vivo Persistence, Trafficking, and Functional Durability Trials frequently stall or fail due to toxicity (such as cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity), inconsistent manufacturing, or inability to meet evolving regulatory standards for advanced therapies. Challenges in production, supply chain, and quality validation can delay or halt progress despite early efficacy signals Even when cell products are successfully infused, they may not reach the right tissues in sufficient numbers, fail to persist, or become functionally exhausted over time. Inadequate product fitness (for example, poor-quality cells at the start or cells not in an ideal state) and continuous antigen stimulation can drive T-cell exhaustion and loss of anti-disease activity Many programs fail due to antigen escape, where disease cells alter or lose target antigens. Additionally, heterogeneous antigen expression makes it difficult to identify targets specific to diseased cells without affecting healthy tissue Target Antigen Instability and Disease Heterogeneity Biological and Immunological Barriers

This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com This presentation is non-exhaustive. For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com INSIGHTS CORNER Cell Therapy: Hematological Malignancies Vs Solid Tumor Antigen Heterogeneity: Solid tumors are highly heterogeneous, meaning cancer cells within the same tumor or between tumors in one patient can express different levels of target antigens. This variability makes it difficult to identify a single tumor-associated antigen for CAR-T therapy, often leading to antigen escape, incomplete tumor killing, and potential relapse. Tumor Microenvironment The TME suppresses immune activity through inhibitory cells and cytokines (e.g., TGF-β, IL-10), limiting T-cell function. In solid tumors, a dense and structured environment restricts CAR-T infiltration and activity. In contrast, hematological TMEs are more diffuse and dynamic enabling continuous cell interactions but also supporting immune evasion and resistance. Cell Trafficking & Physical Barriers CAR-T cells need to effectively reach, infiltrate, and persist at tumor sites to function. In blood cancers, they circulate freely and easily interact with tumor cells. However, solid tumors create physical barriers like dense stroma and abnormal vasculature that limit cell entry. Tumor architecture further restricts deep penetration into the tumor core. As a result, CAR-T cell activity is significantly reduced in solid tumors. T-cell Exhaustion T-cell exhaustion is more pronounced in solid tumors due to continuous antigen exposure and an immunosuppressive microenvironment. This leads to increased inhibitory receptors (e.g., PD-1, CTLA-4, TIM-3) and reduced effector function. As a result, CAR-T cells show diminished cytotoxic activity and persistence. In contrast, lower exhaustion in hematological malignancies allows sustained activity and improved therapeutic efficacy. Safety concerns CAR-T therapies in hematological malignancies commonly cause CRS and ICANS, which are usually manageable with proper treatment. In contrast, solid tumors carry higher risks of on-target, off-tumor toxicity due to shared antigen expression with normal tissues. This can damage vital organs, making safety a major challenge in solid tumor settings. Cell persistence and optimisation In hematological malignancies, CAR-T cells show strong expansion and long-term persistence, especially with early-memory T-cell enrichment. In solid tumors, persistence is limited due to T-cell exhaustion and TME-driven dysfunction. To address this, next-generation approaches include armored CAR-T cells and dominant-negative TGF-β receptors. These strategies aim to enhance durability and are showing early clinical promise. Abbreviations: CRS: Cytokine Release Syndrome, ICANS: Immune Effector Cell-Associated Neurotoxicity Syndrome

hope for patients with rare disorders and hard-to-treat cancers lacking other options, meeting key unmet needs • Expanding pipelines beyond hematology: Numerous clinical trials are actively exploring cell therapies in autoimmune diseases and immunology • Single-Treatment Cure Potential: Certain once-incurable diseases are now curable • Alignment with personalized medicine: Autologous therapies customized for individual patients • High cost: With therapies costing hundreds of thousands to millions $ per dose, strain healthcare systems and limit equitable access • Complex manufacturing and supply chain: Cell therapies as "living" drugs, demand complex cold-chain logistics, manual manufacturing prone to costly failures, uncertain biological integration, and intricate supply chains for quality and efficacy • Side effects: Triggers immune side effects and severe reactions like CRS or ICANS, while allogeneic therapies risk graft- versus-host disease • Expansion into solid tumor: After a decade modest progress in solid tumor, cell therapies are now showing promise in tough cases like glioblastoma, with TILs and TCR-T technologies gaining potential • AI-driven personalization revolution: accelerating therapy development, enhancing precision and safety, and reducing the time required for clinical trials • Innovative Payment Models: Payers test outcomes-based payments and installments to manage high-cost, boosting access and cutting risks • Allogeneic "Off-the-Shelf" revolution: Enable scalable, uniform manufacturing that lowers costs and speeds up patient treatment • Regulatory and reimbursement uncertainty: Evolving standards, regional differences, and payer pushback on pricing create commercial and development risk • Physician & Patient Adoption: Doctors skip risky cell therapies for long-term illnesses if safer treatments work; patients avoid them due to high costs, long hospital time, and prep steps when cheaper options exist • Competition from other modalities: Competition from ADCs and BiTE antibodies, which enable straightforward drug administration SWOT Analysis: Cell Therapy

For additional details or clarifications, please feel free to contact us at bd@octavusconsulting.com INSIGHTS CORNER Market Pricing & Reimbursement US payers use diverse, innovative payment models for cell and gene therapies to manage high upfront costs, share financial risk, and preserve patient access. Innovative approaches like outcomes-based agreements link reimbursement to clinical success, enhancing affordability and accountability. • US access is shaped by a multi-payer system like Medicare, Medicaid and commercial insurers, each use different coverage and payment pathways • For FY 2025, inpatient cases involving CAR-T therapy are classified under MS-DRG 018, with a base reimbursement amount of $269,139 • The base payment will increase by 17% to $314,231 in FY 2026, up from $269,139 in FY 2025 for inpatient CAR-T treatment Market Context • Research findings in 2024 shows median overall costs above $600,000, with 8.5% of patients exceeding $1M. CAR-T therapies such as KYMRIAH and YESCARTA are priced at $373,000 to $475,000 per infusion, while ABECMA and CARVYKTI exceed $450,000 to $465,000, with total patient costs often surpassing $1M after additional hospitalization and management cost in 2026 • In 2024, under Medicare, CAR-T therapy claims averaged $498,723 in inpatient settings ranging from $276,138 to $1,066,524, compared to $414,393 in outpatient settings ranging from $276,980 to $849,878 Price Level/Cost Burden Implemented Models Pros Cons Outcome Based Agreement (OBA)/Value Based Contracts • Payers pay only if outcomes are achieved; lowers risk of ineffective high-cost therapy • Difficult to agree on measurable, clinically meaningful endpoints and timelines • Patient follow-up is hard (e.g., plan switching affects data continuity) Warranty Model • Reimburses costs for suboptimal outcomes if the treatment does not work as expected • Do not address upfront affordability • Requires tracking and identifying non-responding patients Subscription Model • Fixed subscription fee provides stable and manageable budget impact • Spreads financial risk across populations and multiple payers • Payers may incur extra costs regardless of actual usage • May shift risk unnecessarily if payer can already manage it internally Payment Over Time/Installment Model • Spreads high upfront costs into smaller payments, making it easier for smaller payers to manage budgets • Less favored by larger payers, who prefer upfront payment within a single budget cycle, and it is not linked to patient outcomes Cell and Gene Therapy (CGT) Access Model • CMS-led negotiation, funding, and technical support for states • Helps address outcomes tracking and reporting challenges • Limited by scope as currently focused mainly on sickle cell disease therapies Note: Some models are still in pilot or partially implemented stages but are grouped under implemented models for simplicityAbbreviations: MS-DRGs: Medicare Severity Diagnosis Related Groups
